The **La Paz Department** of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") comprises 133,985 square kilometres (51,732 sq mi) with a 2024 [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census") population of 3,022,566 inhabitants. It is situated at the western border of Bolivia, sharing [Lake Titicaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca "Lake Titicaca") with the neighboring [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"). It contains the [Cordillera Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Real_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Real (Bolivia)") mountain range, which reaches altitudes of 6.6 kilometers (22,000 ft). Northeast of the Cordillera Real are the _[Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yungas "Yungas")_, the steep eastern slopes of the [Andes Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") that make the transition to the [Amazon River basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River") to the northeast. The capital of the department is the [city of La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") and is the administrative city and [seat of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_of_government "Seat of government")/national [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") of Bolivia.

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Government")]

The chief executive office of [Bolivia's departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia") (since May 2010) is the [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"); before then, the office was called the [Prefect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefect "Prefect"), and until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [President of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") and then the governor is elected by the voters. The current governor, Santos Quispe, was elected on 11 April 2021 and took office on 3 May.

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, known as the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The La Paz Assembly has 45 members including five indigenous / natives minority representatives.

The **La Paz Department** of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") comprises 133,985 square kilometres (51,732 sq mi) with a 2024 [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census") population of 3,022,566 inhabitants. It is situated at the western border of Bolivia, sharing [Lake Titicaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca "Lake Titicaca") with the neighboring [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"). It contains the [Cordillera Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Real_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Real (Bolivia)") mountain range, which reaches altitudes of 6.6 kilometers (22,000 ft). Northeast of the Cordillera Real are the _[Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yungas "Yungas")_, the steep eastern slopes of the [Andes Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") that make the transition to the [Amazon River basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River") to the northeast. The capital of the department is the [city of La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") and is the administrative city and [seat of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_of_government "Seat of government")/national [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") of Bolivia.

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Government")]

The chief executive office of [Bolivia's departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia") (since May 2010) is the [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"); before then, the office was called the [Prefect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefect "Prefect"), and until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [President of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") and then the governor is elected by the voters. The current governor, Santos Quispe, was elected on 11 April 2021 and took office on 3 May.

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, known as the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The La Paz Assembly has 45 members including five indigenous / natives minority representatives.

**Beni** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˈbeni]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")), sometimes **El Beni**, is a northeastern [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia") of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), in the lowlands region of the country. It is the second-largest department in the country (after Santa Cruz), covering 213,564 square kilometers (82,458 sq mi), and it was created by supreme decree on November 18, 1842, during the administration of General [José Ballivián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Ballivi%C3%A1n "José Ballivián"). Its capital is [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad,_Bolivia "Trinidad, Bolivia").

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The name of the department was given by President José Ballivián in honor of the [Beni River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_River "Beni River"). The name Beni is derived from the [Movima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movima_language "Movima language") word _ben’i_, meaning “grasslands”. However, a manuscript by Friar [Nicolás Armentia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Armentia_Ugarte "Nicolás Armentia Ugarte") states that the word Beni comes from the [Tacanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacanan_languages "Tacanan languages") languages, in which it means “wind.”[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-3)

## Population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Population")]

With a population of 488,260, according to the 2024 census, Beni is the second least-populated of the nine [departments of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia"), after [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-:0-4)

Although Beni is rich in natural resources, the poverty level of its inhabitants is high, mainly as a result of centuries of exploitation of native populations by European-descended elites[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. The main economic activities are agriculture, timber, and cattle. In addition, an [underground economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_economy "Underground economy") linked to illegal narcotics activities flourished in the area during the last decades of the 20th century, with many [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine "Cocaine") laboratories hidden behind the façade of remote cattle ranches.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-:0-4)

The Beni region is wide and flat, featuring many large [mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound "Mound") connected by straight earthen [causeways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeways "Causeways"), which are believed by researchers to have been built by ancient inhabitants. The earthwork mounds provide raised living areas and enable the growth of trees that could not survive otherwise in the frequently flooded lowland area. In the 21st century, archeologists and anthropologists such as Americans Clark Erickson and William Balée, respectively, believe these earthwork structures are evidence of a large and sophisticated indigenous civilization that flourished for thousands of years before European colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-mann-5)

The first European settlers in this area were Spanish Jesuit missionaries during the 18th century, sent to convert the native inhabitants, chiefly in the southern half of the department. The religious origins of many of the Beni's towns can be attested to by the centrality of the local church in most of the communities, and in the very names of the towns: Trinidad, Santa Ana, San Borja, Reyes, etc. Today, the Beni region is the seat of the [Roman Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of El Beni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Apostolic_Vicariate_of_El_Beni "Roman Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of El Beni").

The importance of cattle ranching is prominent in the regional culture. Cowboys, or "[vaqueros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaquero "Vaquero")", still play an important role in Beni society, comprising a large portion of the working class. Other industries significant to the region include logging, small-scale fishing and hunting, farming, and in recent years, eco-tourism.

Though the Beni lies in the southern reaches of the Amazon Basin, an area renowned for tropical disease, the population has fewer health problems than in the Andes Region, especially those related to malnutrition.

The inhabitants (Benianos) are mostly descendants of Cruceños (people from [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra")) who streamed north following the course of navigable rivers, and native peoples.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Beniano diet consists largely of rice, bananas, beef, and fish. Some popular dishes include Majao, Masaco, and others, many featuring cured/salted meats.

The majority of the population in Beni is mestizo. The white/mestizo Benianos have traditionally been mistrustful, and often somewhat contemptuous, of Andean culture. They identify as being lighter skinned and of more Spanish ancestry than the Quechua and Aymara-speaking populations of the highlands. Considerable resentment existed against the central government, which allegedly did very little to build roads or integrate the Beni into the economy and political life of Bolivia. These attitudes persisted although Beni residents benefited greatly by the Agrarian Reform instituted following the 1952 Revolution, with many citizens gaining ownership of significant tracts of land. Most of these turned to cattle ranching. The absence of a reliable road linking the department to the main centers of power in the country (owing to the difficult terrain) continued to contribute to the Benianos' perception of isolation, as did a downturn in the cattle industry. As a result, both the white/mestizo population and departmental authorities supported the Santa Cruz-led effort to federalize the country and devolve powers to the departments at the expense of the central government. Considerable social unrest took place in 2007 and 2008, leading some to consider separatism as plausible.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 10: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(November 2012)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

Beni was a very important center of a pre-Columbian civilization known as the [hydraulic culture of Las Lomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_de_Moxos_(archaeology) "Llanos de Moxos (archaeology)") (the hills), a culture that constructed over 20,000 man-made artificial hills, all interconnected by thousands of square kilometers of aqueducts, channels, embankments, artificial lakes and lagoons, as well as terraces. Between about 4000 BC (and probably earlier as this date is taken from ceramics that have been carbon dated) and the 13th century AD this region was settled by sophisticated and organized groups of human societies. Their civil structures were based, both environmentally and economically, on the use of specific environmental characteristics (such as the use of aquatic plants as fertilizer, and enormous fishing systems they constructed). Miles of these channels and man-made earthworks are visible from the air when flying over Beni.

When the Spanish arrived, the region had already been in decline for about three hundred years. However, this is where many products that are now used worldwide originated in native cultivation: among them [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), [peanuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut "Peanut"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava") (manioc), [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") and [sweet potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato "Sweet potato"). The Spanish initially were intensely interested in this area. During the first century of colonization, they believed the mythical city of _[El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Dorado "El Dorado")_ (also known as _Paititi_) could be found in this region. However, they never found this legendary city of gold and they soon lost interest in the area, which would remain marginalized for several centuries after.

Between the 19th and 20th centuries northern Beni became Bolivia's rubber capital. The abundance of rubber trees attracted many people to the region, many of them adventurers and workers (many of whom were indigenous) to work in the huge rubber plantations that arose. The worldwide demand for rubber rose with industrialization and the use of automotive vehicles. For decades this was one of the most active, dynamic regions of Bolivia. [Cachuela Esperanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachuela_Esperanza "Cachuela Esperanza") was an important center for rubber exports as it is located along the shores of the [Beni River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_River "Beni River"). As a measure of its success, it had one of the best-equipped hospitals in Bolivia at the end of the 19th century. But these enormous rubber plantations all but disappeared by the end of the Second World War, as developers had been cultivating rubber introduced to plantations of Southeast Asia and Africa. Today many of the properties have been converted to cattle ranches. Only some small rubber producers still use the river to transport their production.

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Government")]

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

The chief executive office of [Bolivia departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia") (since May 2010) is the governor, who is elected to office; until then, the office was called the prefect. Until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [president of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). As of 2011 Beni had an interim governor, Haysen Ribera Leigue, who was selected by the Departmental Legislative Assembly on 16 December 2011.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-Suspendido-7) Governor Ernesto Suárez Sattori, who was elected on 4 April 2010, was suspended following his indictment for irregular expenditures related to a power plant in [San Borja, Beni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Borja_(Beni) "San Borja (Beni)"), in compliance with a Bolivian legal mandate that indicted officials may not continue to serve.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-Suspendido-7) As a replacement for the governor Carmelo Lens was elected in the [special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_special_gubernatorial_election,_2013 "Beni special gubernatorial election, 2013") on 20 January 2013. The current governor, Alejandro Unzueta of the MTS was elected on 7 March 2021.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-eab-8)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Beni "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010. The leading party in the twenty-eight member assembly is [Beni First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_First "Beni First"), with 11 seats. The [Movement towards Socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") (MAS-IPSP) holds 10 seats, and the [Revolutionary Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Nationalist_Movement "Revolutionary Nationalist Movement") (MNR) holds 3 seats. Two seats each were selected by indigenous people and by peasants through _[usos y costumbres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usos\_y\_costumbres "Usos y costumbres")_. In alliance with the indigenous and peasant representatives, the MAS-IPSP controls the presidency of the Assembly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-11) The three MNR representatives and their alternates were derecognized by the national party in 2010 when they backed MAS-IPSP policies and leadership.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-12)

The December 2011 suspension of Governor Ernesto Suarez was backed by 15 votes, including the MAS and MNR delegations, and two indigenous or campesino representatives. Two members of the assembly were also indicted simultaneously and replaced by their alternates: Sonia Suárez Araúz (MNR) was replaced by Juan Carlos Herrera; and Carlos Navia Ribera (MAS-IPSP) was replaced by Tatiana Paniagua Zabala.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-13) The interim governor was also a member of the Assembly.

### National Congress

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: National Congress")]

In the [National Congress of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_Bolivia "National Congress of Bolivia") Beni elects nine out of 130 members of the _Cámara de Diputados_ (Chamber of Deputies), and four members of the _Cámara de Senadores_ (Chamber of Senators).

Beni's weather is tropical and humid, with a prevalence of warm to hot temperatures.

Beni borders upon [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") to the northeast, and the departments of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the southeast, [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") to the west, [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department") to the northwest, and [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department "Cochabamba Department") to the south. Beni's territory is mainly covered by [rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest") (particularly the northern and eastern portions of the department) and [pampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa "Pampa") (notably the grassland Moxos Plain to the south, closer to the Andean reaches). Much of Beni is at about 155 meters above sea level. Although most of the department is flat, along the border with La Paz there are two sierra chains called Eva Eva and Pelado. Beni is criss-crossed by numerous rivers, all of which are Amazon tributaries. The largest of these are the Iténez (also known as Guaporé), Mamoré, Madre de Dios, Madera, Yata, Ivón, Machupo, Itonama, Baures, San Martín, San Miguel, San Simón, Negro, Sécure, Yacuma, Maniquí, Ibare and Apere, all of which are navigable. Beni also has numerous lakes and lagoons. The most important of these are: [Laguna Suárez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Su%C3%A1rez "Laguna Suárez"), [Rogagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogagua?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rogagua (page does not exist)"), Rogaguado, San Luis, San Pablo, [Huachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huachi_Lake "Huachi Lake"), Huatunas, Yusala, Huachuna, Agua Clara, Ginebra, La Dichosa, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Bolivia "Laguna Bolivia"), Navidad, Las Abras, Larga, Maracaibo and [Aquiles Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquiles_Lake "Aquiles Lake").

### Flora and fauna

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Flora and fauna")]

[![Image 13: Map of Beni showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Beni%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Beni%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Beni,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Beni, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Capybara_Bolivie.jpg/250px-Capybara_Bolivie.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capybara_Bolivie.jpg)

[Capybara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara "Capybara") family in the region of [Rurrenabaque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rurrenabaque "Rurrenabaque"), Beni Dept.

In the region's many rivers over 400 species of fish have been found. Trinidad has an entire museum, the _Museo Ictícola_, dedicated to Beni's fish fauna which is the third largest of its type in South America. The most commonly fished and consumed species are [pacú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac%C3%BA "Pacú"), [tambaquí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambaqu%C3%AD?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tambaquí (page does not exist)"), [surubí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surub%C3%AD "Surubí"), palometa (a type of [piranha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piranha "Piranha")), sábalo, bagre (catfish), and blanquillo. Alligators are also hunted for their leather and meat, which is considered a delicacy and is a common part of meals in Beni. Beni now also exports huge amounts of lumber, although over the past 20 years the government of Bolivia has worked with numerous international entities and NGOs to certify its lumber concessions and all lumber exported must be accompanied by certificates of origin.

Conservation funding tied to Bolivia’s 1987 debt-for-nature swap, implemented by [Conservation International Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_International_Bolivia "Conservation International Bolivia"), supported conservation in the Beni region, including the Beni Biosphere Reserve.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-CIBolivia_WB_DebtSwaps_1993-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-CIBolivia_LATimes_DebtSwap_1987-15)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate")]

Beni is hot and humid during most of the year with an annual rainfall average between 1,000–4,000 mm (39–157 in). It is one of the wettest regions in Bolivia, with more wetlands than the better-known [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal"). During the winter (June and July) the weather can be cool and winds blowing northward from the South Pole and Argentina's Patagonia region can cause temperatures to drop quite drastically very quickly.

## Agriculture and livestock

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Agriculture and livestock")]

Because of its climate and rich soils, the department is Bolivia's second largest agricultural center after Santa Cruz. There are extensive fields of corn, yucca (manioc), sunflowers, rice, and many tropical fruits such as cacao (from which chocolate is made), Brazil nuts (one of the regions main crops and exports), soybeans, bananas, maracuya, guayaba, papaya, and many other citrus fruits. Coffee is also grown extensively. Beni is also the second Bolivia's largest cattle-ranching region. Official estimates calculate there are anywhere between 2 and 2.5 million heads of cattle throughout the year. Most of these are turned out to pasture and thus are naturally fed.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Demography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Demography")]

According to the 2024 Bolivian census, the population of the Department of Beni is 488,260 inhabitants.

### Historical population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Historical population")]

Censuses prior to 1882 are not entirely accurate or reliable, as they provide only estimates and do not precisely reflect the departmental population of that period. Only from 1882 onward, after the end of the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific") are precise population data available for each department of Bolivia.

The population of the department increased by almost sevenfold between 1950 and 2024:

### Immigration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Immigration")]

As with other departments, the Department of Beni has received immigrants from different parts of Bolivia as well as from other countries around the world.

Residents originally from La Paz have become one of the largest communities within the department. Other significant groups include residents from Santa Cruz, Pando, and Cochabamba.

### Population density

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Population density")]

The Department of Beni is one of the least densely populated departments in Bolivia. Its low population density is due to its vast territory of forests, plains, and areas that are difficult to access.

*   Area: Approximately 213,564 km², making it the second-largest department in the country.
*   Population: According to the 2024 Bolivian census, the department had approximately 488,000 inhabitants.
*   Population density: About 2.8 inhabitants per km², reflecting a low concentration of population, mainly due to the region’s geographic characteristics (forests, rivers, and wetlands).

### Urban and rural population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Urban and rural population")]

*   Urban population: Approximately 356,661 (73%) of Beni’s population lives in urban areas, mainly in the city of [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad,_Beni "Trinidad, Beni") and other important localities such as [Riberalta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riberalta "Riberalta"), [Guayaramerín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaramer%C3%ADn "Guayaramerín"), and [San Borja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Borja,_Bolivia "San Borja, Bolivia").
*   Rural population: Around 131,599 (27%) lives in dispersed rural areas, where Indigenous communities play an important role.

### Migration and growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Migration and growth")]

The Department of Beni has experienced relatively low population growth compared to other departments of Bolivia. Limited employment opportunities and living conditions in many rural areas have encouraged internal migration, especially toward more industrialized departments such as Santa Cruz and La Paz.

### Age distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Age distribution")]

The age structure of the Department of Beni reflects a young population, similar to other regions of Bolivia. However, in rural areas, birth rates are higher than in urban zones.

*   **Children and adolescents (0–14 years):** totalled 161,402 or around 33% of the population
*   **Young adults (15–39 years):** totalled 200,476 or approximately 41%
*   **Older adults (40 years and over):** totalled 126,382, the remaining 26%

### Challenges and development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Challenges and development")]

The department faces significant development challenges, including a lack of adequate infrastructure and limited access to education and health services in the most remote areas. These constraints have contributed to maintaining low population density and a demographic structure that remains predominantly rural.

**Beni** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˈbeni]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")), sometimes **El Beni**, is a northeastern [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia") of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), in the lowlands region of the country. It is the second-largest department in the country (after Santa Cruz), covering 213,564 square kilometers (82,458 sq mi), and it was created by supreme decree on November 18, 1842, during the administration of General [José Ballivián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Ballivi%C3%A1n "José Ballivián"). Its capital is [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad,_Bolivia "Trinidad, Bolivia").

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The name of the department was given by President José Ballivián in honor of the [Beni River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_River "Beni River"). The name Beni is derived from the [Movima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movima_language "Movima language") word _ben’i_, meaning “grasslands”. However, a manuscript by Friar [Nicolás Armentia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Armentia_Ugarte "Nicolás Armentia Ugarte") states that the word Beni comes from the [Tacanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacanan_languages "Tacanan languages") languages, in which it means “wind.”[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-3)

## Population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Population")]

With a population of 488,260, according to the 2024 census, Beni is the second least-populated of the nine [departments of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Bolivia "Departments of Bolivia"), after [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-:0-4)

Although Beni is rich in natural resources, the poverty level of its inhabitants is high, mainly as a result of centuries of exploitation of native populations by European-descended elites[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. The main economic activities are agriculture, timber, and cattle. In addition, an [underground economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_economy "Underground economy") linked to illegal narcotics activities flourished in the area during the last decades of the 20th century, with many [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine "Cocaine") laboratories hidden behind the façade of remote cattle ranches.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-:0-4)

The Beni region is wide and flat, featuring many large [mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound "Mound") connected by straight earthen [causeways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeways "Causeways"), which are believed by researchers to have been built by ancient inhabitants. The earthwork mounds provide raised living areas and enable the growth of trees that could not survive otherwise in the frequently flooded lowland area. In the 21st century, archeologists and anthropologists such as Americans Clark Erickson and William Balée, respectively, believe these earthwork structures are evidence of a large and sophisticated indigenous civilization that flourished for thousands of years before European colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-mann-5)

The first European settlers in this area were Spanish Jesuit missionaries during the 18th century, sent to convert the native inhabitants, chiefly in the southern half of the department. The religious origins of many of the Beni's towns can be attested to by the centrality of the local church in most of the communities, and in the very names of the towns: Trinidad, Santa Ana, San Borja, Reyes, etc. Today, the Beni region is the seat of the [Roman Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of El Beni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Apostolic_Vicariate_of_El_Beni "Roman Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of El Beni").

The importance of cattle ranching is prominent in the regional culture. Cowboys, or "[vaqueros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaquero "Vaquero")", still play an important role in Beni society, comprising a large portion of the working class. Other industries significant to the region include logging, small-scale fishing and hunting, farming, and in recent years, eco-tourism.

Though the Beni lies in the southern reaches of the Amazon Basin, an area renowned for tropical disease, the population has fewer health problems than in the Andes Region, especially those related to malnutrition.

The inhabitants (Benianos) are mostly descendants of Cruceños (people from [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra")) who streamed north following the course of navigable rivers, and native peoples.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Beniano diet consists largely of rice, bananas, beef, and fish. Some popular dishes include Majao, Masaco, and others, many featuring cured/salted meats.

The majority of the population in Beni is mestizo. The white/mestizo Benianos have traditionally been mistrustful, and often somewhat contemptuous, of Andean culture. They identify as being lighter skinned and of more Spanish ancestry than the Quechua and Aymara-speaking populations of the highlands. Considerable resentment existed against the central government, which allegedly did very little to build roads or integrate the Beni into the economy and political life of Bolivia. These attitudes persisted although Beni residents benefited greatly by the Agrarian Reform instituted following the 1952 Revolution, with many citizens gaining ownership of significant tracts of land. Most of these turned to cattle ranching. The absence of a reliable road linking the department to the main centers of power in the country (owing to the difficult terrain) continued to contribute to the Benianos' perception of isolation, as did a downturn in the cattle industry. As a result, both the white/mestizo population and departmental authorities supported the Santa Cruz-led effort to federalize the country and devolve powers to the departments at the expense of the central government. Considerable social unrest took place in 2007 and 2008, leading some to consider separatism as plausible.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 10: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Beni_Department "Special:EditPage/Beni Department") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(November 2012)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

Beni was a very important center of a pre-Columbian civilization known as the [hydraulic culture of Las Lomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_de_Moxos_(archaeology) "Llanos de Moxos (archaeology)") (the hills), a culture that constructed over 20,000 man-made artificial hills, all interconnected by thousands of square kilometers of aqueducts, channels, embankments, artificial lakes and lagoons, as well as terraces. Between about 4000 BC (and probably earlier as this date is taken from ceramics that have been carbon dated) and the 13th century AD this region was settled by sophisticated and organized groups of human societies. Their civil structures were based, both environmentally and economically, on the use of specific environmental characteristics (such as the use of aquatic plants as fertilizer, and enormous fishing systems they constructed). Miles of these channels and man-made earthworks are visible from the air when flying over Beni.

When the Spanish arrived, the region had already been in decline for about three hundred years. However, this is where many products that are now used worldwide originated in native cultivation: among them [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), [peanuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut "Peanut"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava") (manioc), [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") and [sweet potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato "Sweet potato"). The Spanish initially were intensely interested in this area. During the first century of colonization, they believed the mythical city of _[El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Dorado "El Dorado")_ (also known as _Paititi_) could be found in this region. However, they never found this legendary city of gold and they soon lost interest in the area, which would remain marginalized for several centuries after.

Between the 19th and 20th centuries northern Beni became Bolivia's rubber capital. The abundance of rubber trees attracted many people to the region, many of them adventurers and workers (many of whom were indigenous) to work in the huge rubber plantations that arose. The worldwide demand for rubber rose with industrialization and the use of automotive vehicles. For decades this was one of the most active, dynamic regions of Bolivia. [Cachuela Esperanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachuela_Esperanza "Cachuela Esperanza") was an important center for rubber exports as it is located along the shores of the [Beni River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_River "Beni River"). As a measure of its success, it had one of the best-equipped hospitals in Bolivia at the end of the 19th century. But these enormous rubber plantations all but disappeared by the end of the Second World War, as developers had been cultivating rubber introduced to plantations of Southeast Asia and Africa. Today many of the properties have been converted to cattle ranches. Only some small rubber producers still use the river to transport their production.

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Beni "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010. The leading party in the twenty-eight member assembly is [Beni First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_First "Beni First"), with 11 seats. The [Movement towards Socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") (MAS-IPSP) holds 10 seats, and the [Revolutionary Nationalist Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Nationalist_Movement "Revolutionary Nationalist Movement") (MNR) holds 3 seats. Two seats each were selected by indigenous people and by peasants through _[usos y costumbres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usos\_y\_costumbres "Usos y costumbres")_. In alliance with the indigenous and peasant representatives, the MAS-IPSP controls the presidency of the Assembly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-11) The three MNR representatives and their alternates were derecognized by the national party in 2010 when they backed MAS-IPSP policies and leadership.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-12)

The December 2011 suspension of Governor Ernesto Suarez was backed by 15 votes, including the MAS and MNR delegations, and two indigenous or campesino representatives. Two members of the assembly were also indicted simultaneously and replaced by their alternates: Sonia Suárez Araúz (MNR) was replaced by Juan Carlos Herrera; and Carlos Navia Ribera (MAS-IPSP) was replaced by Tatiana Paniagua Zabala.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-13) The interim governor was also a member of the Assembly.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Geography")]

[Beni savanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_savanna "Beni savanna")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/San_Ignacio_de_Moxos_2.jpg/250px-San_Ignacio_de_Moxos_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:San_Ignacio_de_Moxos_2.jpg)

[San Ignacio de Moxos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Ignacio_de_Moxos "San Ignacio de Moxos")

Beni's weather is tropical and humid, with a prevalence of warm to hot temperatures.

Beni borders upon [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") to the northeast, and the departments of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the southeast, [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") to the west, [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department") to the northwest, and [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department "Cochabamba Department") to the south. Beni's territory is mainly covered by [rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest") (particularly the northern and eastern portions of the department) and [pampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa "Pampa") (notably the grassland Moxos Plain to the south, closer to the Andean reaches). Much of Beni is at about 155 meters above sea level. Although most of the department is flat, along the border with La Paz there are two sierra chains called Eva Eva and Pelado. Beni is criss-crossed by numerous rivers, all of which are Amazon tributaries. The largest of these are the Iténez (also known as Guaporé), Mamoré, Madre de Dios, Madera, Yata, Ivón, Machupo, Itonama, Baures, San Martín, San Miguel, San Simón, Negro, Sécure, Yacuma, Maniquí, Ibare and Apere, all of which are navigable. Beni also has numerous lakes and lagoons. The most important of these are: [Laguna Suárez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Su%C3%A1rez "Laguna Suárez"), [Rogagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogagua?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rogagua (page does not exist)"), Rogaguado, San Luis, San Pablo, [Huachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huachi_Lake "Huachi Lake"), Huatunas, Yusala, Huachuna, Agua Clara, Ginebra, La Dichosa, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Bolivia "Laguna Bolivia"), Navidad, Las Abras, Larga, Maracaibo and [Aquiles Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquiles_Lake "Aquiles Lake").

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Capybara_Bolivie.jpg/250px-Capybara_Bolivie.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capybara_Bolivie.jpg)

[Capybara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara "Capybara") family in the region of [Rurrenabaque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rurrenabaque "Rurrenabaque"), Beni Dept.

In the region's many rivers over 400 species of fish have been found. Trinidad has an entire museum, the _Museo Ictícola_, dedicated to Beni's fish fauna which is the third largest of its type in South America. The most commonly fished and consumed species are [pacú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac%C3%BA "Pacú"), [tambaquí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambaqu%C3%AD?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tambaquí (page does not exist)"), [surubí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surub%C3%AD "Surubí"), palometa (a type of [piranha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piranha "Piranha")), sábalo, bagre (catfish), and blanquillo. Alligators are also hunted for their leather and meat, which is considered a delicacy and is a common part of meals in Beni. Beni now also exports huge amounts of lumber, although over the past 20 years the government of Bolivia has worked with numerous international entities and NGOs to certify its lumber concessions and all lumber exported must be accompanied by certificates of origin.

Conservation funding tied to Bolivia’s 1987 debt-for-nature swap, implemented by [Conservation International Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_International_Bolivia "Conservation International Bolivia"), supported conservation in the Beni region, including the Beni Biosphere Reserve.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-CIBolivia_WB_DebtSwaps_1993-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department#cite_note-CIBolivia_LATimes_DebtSwap_1987-15)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate")]

Beni is hot and humid during most of the year with an annual rainfall average between 1,000–4,000 mm (39–157 in). It is one of the wettest regions in Bolivia, with more wetlands than the better-known [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal"). During the winter (June and July) the weather can be cool and winds blowing northward from the South Pole and Argentina's Patagonia region can cause temperatures to drop quite drastically very quickly.

## Agriculture and livestock

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Agriculture and livestock")]

Because of its climate and rich soils, the department is Bolivia's second largest agricultural center after Santa Cruz. There are extensive fields of corn, yucca (manioc), sunflowers, rice, and many tropical fruits such as cacao (from which chocolate is made), Brazil nuts (one of the regions main crops and exports), soybeans, bananas, maracuya, guayaba, papaya, and many other citrus fruits. Coffee is also grown extensively. Beni is also the second Bolivia's largest cattle-ranching region. Official estimates calculate there are anywhere between 2 and 2.5 million heads of cattle throughout the year. Most of these are turned out to pasture and thus are naturally fed.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Immigration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Immigration")]

As with other departments, the Department of Beni has received immigrants from different parts of Bolivia as well as from other countries around the world.

Residents originally from La Paz have become one of the largest communities within the department. Other significant groups include residents from Santa Cruz, Pando, and Cochabamba.

### Population density

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Population density")]

The Department of Beni is one of the least densely populated departments in Bolivia. Its low population density is due to its vast territory of forests, plains, and areas that are difficult to access.

*   Area: Approximately 213,564 km², making it the second-largest department in the country.
*   Population: According to the 2024 Bolivian census, the department had approximately 488,000 inhabitants.
*   Population density: About 2.8 inhabitants per km², reflecting a low concentration of population, mainly due to the region’s geographic characteristics (forests, rivers, and wetlands).

### Urban and rural population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Urban and rural population")]

*   Urban population: Approximately 356,661 (73%) of Beni’s population lives in urban areas, mainly in the city of [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad,_Beni "Trinidad, Beni") and other important localities such as [Riberalta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riberalta "Riberalta"), [Guayaramerín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaramer%C3%ADn "Guayaramerín"), and [San Borja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Borja,_Bolivia "San Borja, Bolivia").
*   Rural population: Around 131,599 (27%) lives in dispersed rural areas, where Indigenous communities play an important role.

### Migration and growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Migration and growth")]

The Department of Beni has experienced relatively low population growth compared to other departments of Bolivia. Limited employment opportunities and living conditions in many rural areas have encouraged internal migration, especially toward more industrialized departments such as Santa Cruz and La Paz.

### Age distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Age distribution")]

The age structure of the Department of Beni reflects a young population, similar to other regions of Bolivia. However, in rural areas, birth rates are higher than in urban zones.

*   **Children and adolescents (0–14 years):** totalled 161,402 or around 33% of the population
*   **Young adults (15–39 years):** totalled 200,476 or approximately 41%
*   **Older adults (40 years and over):** totalled 126,382, the remaining 26%

### Challenges and development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beni_Department&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Challenges and development")]

The department faces significant development challenges, including a lack of adequate infrastructure and limited access to education and health services in the most remote areas. These constraints have contributed to maintaining low population density and a demographic structure that remains predominantly rural.

[Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") is a [unitary state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") consisting of nine **[departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(administrative_division) "Department (administrative division)")** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_). Departments are the primary subdivisions of Bolivia, and possess certain rights under the [Constitution of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"). Each department is represented in the [Plurinational Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurinational_Legislative_Assembly "Plurinational Legislative Assembly")—a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") legislature consisting of the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Each department is represented by four Senators, while Deputies are awarded to each department in proportion to their total population.

Out of the nine departments, [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)") was originally the most populous, with 2,706,351 inhabitants as of 2012 but the far eastern department of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") has since surpassed it by 2020; Santa Cruz also claims the title as the largest, encompassing 370,621 square kilometres (143,098 mi 2). [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department") is the least populated, with a population of 110,436. The smallest in area is [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department"), encompassing 37,623 square kilometres (14,526 mi 2).

[Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") is a [unitary state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") consisting of nine **[departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(administrative_division) "Department (administrative division)")** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_). Departments are the primary subdivisions of Bolivia, and possess certain rights under the [Constitution of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"). Each department is represented in the [Plurinational Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurinational_Legislative_Assembly "Plurinational Legislative Assembly")—a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") legislature consisting of the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Each department is represented by four Senators, while Deputies are awarded to each department in proportion to their total population.

Out of the nine departments, [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)") was originally the most populous, with 2,706,351 inhabitants as of 2012 but the far eastern department of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") has since surpassed it by 2020; Santa Cruz also claims the title as the largest, encompassing 370,621 square kilometres (143,098 mi 2). [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department") is the least populated, with a population of 110,436. The smallest in area is [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department"), encompassing 37,623 square kilometres (14,526 mi 2).

**Potosí** (Spanish pronunciation:[[potoˈsi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Quechua "Southern Quechua"): _P'utuqsi_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Putusi_) is a department in southwestern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its area is 118,218 km 2 (45,644 sq mi) and its population is 856,419 (2024 census). The capital is the city of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). It is a mostly barren, mountainous region with one large [plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau") to the west, where the largest [salt flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") in the world, [Salar de Uyuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni "Salar de Uyuni"), is located.

[Cerro Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico") was the richest province in the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), providing a great percentage of the [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") that was [shipped to Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleet "Spanish treasure fleet").

Potosi is also the location of the [San Cristóbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Crist%C3%B3bal_mine_(Bolivia) "San Cristóbal mine (Bolivia)") silver, zinc and lead mines, developed by the US company Apex Silver Mines Limited of Colorado and sold in November 2008 to the Japanese [Sumitomo Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation").

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James's_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada,_Bolivia.jpg)

[Laguna Colorada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Colorada "Laguna Colorada") with [flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamingo "Flamingo") in the [Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Avaroa_Andean_Fauna_National_Reserve "Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In March 2023, social organisations in four regions of Potosí, with the support of regional [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAS-IPSP "MAS-IPSP") lawmakers, called for a strike spanning over 72 hours, to force the government to raise infrastructure investments in the department and to receive an increased amount of the profits generated through lithium mining in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-a21-3) Shortly after the strike an agreement with the central government was reached, stipulating the construction of motorways and a cement plant and further discussions about mining conditions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-a21-3)

The chief executive office of Bolivia departments (since May 2010) is the governor; until then, the office was called the prefect, and until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [President of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). The current governor, Jhonny Mamani of the [Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") was elected on 7 March 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-eab-4)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Bolivian_regional_elections "2010 Bolivian regional elections") were held 4 April 2010.

The current executive committee consists of Jacinto Sunagua Dorado as president, Raimunda Cordero Caba as vice-president and Alberto Quispe Mamani as secretary and Blanca Celia Burgos Quispe and Leon Jancko Condori as first and second committee member, respectively.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-5)

**Potosí** (Spanish pronunciation:[[potoˈsi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Quechua "Southern Quechua"): _P'utuqsi_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Putusi_) is a department in southwestern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its area is 118,218 km 2 (45,644 sq mi) and its population is 856,419 (2024 census). The capital is the city of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). It is a mostly barren, mountainous region with one large [plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau") to the west, where the largest [salt flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") in the world, [Salar de Uyuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni "Salar de Uyuni"), is located.

[Cerro Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico") was the richest province in the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), providing a great percentage of the [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") that was [shipped to Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleet "Spanish treasure fleet").

Potosi is also the location of the [San Cristóbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Crist%C3%B3bal_mine_(Bolivia) "San Cristóbal mine (Bolivia)") silver, zinc and lead mines, developed by the US company Apex Silver Mines Limited of Colorado and sold in November 2008 to the Japanese [Sumitomo Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation").

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James's_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada,_Bolivia.jpg)

[Laguna Colorada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Colorada "Laguna Colorada") with [flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamingo "Flamingo") in the [Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Avaroa_Andean_Fauna_National_Reserve "Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In March 2023, social organisations in four regions of Potosí, with the support of regional [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAS-IPSP "MAS-IPSP") lawmakers, called for a strike spanning over 72 hours, to force the government to raise infrastructure investments in the department and to receive an increased amount of the profits generated through lithium mining in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-a21-3) Shortly after the strike an agreement with the central government was reached, stipulating the construction of motorways and a cement plant and further discussions about mining conditions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-a21-3)

## Government

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

The chief executive office of Bolivia departments (since May 2010) is the governor; until then, the office was called the prefect, and until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [President of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). The current governor, Jhonny Mamani of the [Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") was elected on 7 March 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-eab-4)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Bolivian_regional_elections "2010 Bolivian regional elections") were held 4 April 2010.

The current executive committee consists of Jacinto Sunagua Dorado as president, Raimunda Cordero Caba as vice-president and Alberto Quispe Mamani as secretary and Blanca Celia Burgos Quispe and Leon Jancko Condori as first and second committee member, respectively.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department#cite_note-5)

**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Quchapampa Jach'a Suyu_, [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Departamento de Cochabamba_ pronounced[[kotʃaˈβamba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/95/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg "File:ES-pe - Cochabamba.ogg"), [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa Suyu_), from Quechua _qucha_ or _qhucha_, meaning "lake", _pampa_ meaning "plain",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-3) is one of the nine departments of Bolivia. It is known to be the [breadbasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadbasket "Breadbasket") of the country because of its variety of agricultural products from its geographical position. It has an area of 55,631 km 2. Its population in the 2024 census was 2,005,373. Its capital is the city of [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), known as the "City of Eternal Spring" and "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Cochabamba valley has been inhabited for over a thousand years due to its fertile productive soils and climate. Archaeological evidence suggests that the initial valley inhabitants were of various ethnic indigenous groups. [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, Omereque and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at various times before the Spanish arrived.

The first Spanish inhabitant of the Valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of Potosí. The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood of the city.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa was founded on 2 August 1571 by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa. It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food for the mining towns of the relatively nearby Altiplano region, particularly the city of Potosí which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 17th century– funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power at the time. With the silver mining industry in Potosi at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries of existence. The city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786, King Charles III of Spain renamed the city to the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in Oruro by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 mestizos, 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 mulattos and 175 African slaves.

In 2000, Cochabamba was wracked by large-scale protests over the privatisation of the city's water supply, known as the [Water War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Water_War "Cochabamba Water War").

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured. The democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, a former military aide to the Luis García Meza dictatorship of the 1980s, had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's eastern departments in a dispute with President Evo Morales over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions have not been resolved.

In July 2007, a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.

In August 2008, a nationwide referendum was held, and while President Evo Morales had 67% support in Bolivia, the Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters of the department.

In 2018 Cochabamba hosted the 2018 South American Games ODESUR.

Around 74% of Cochabambinos identify as indigenous, while most of the remaining population is mestizo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Cochabamba Department is bordered by [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department") and Potosi Departments to the south, [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department") and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") Departments to the west, Beni Department to the north, and [Santa Cruz Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the east. The borders are formed mainly by rivers, like **Ichilo** to the east, **Rio Grande** to the south and **Cotacajes** to the west.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-5)

[![Image 9: Map of Cochabamba showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Cochabamba, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Geographically and climatically, Cochabamba is one of Bolivia's most diverse regions, with a similar orography and diversity to [La Paz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)"). Cochabamba is made up of a variety of regions. The northern portions of the department, known as the Chapare, is a region of moist [Southwestern Amazonian moist forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Amazonian_moist_forests "Southwestern Amazonian moist forests") with high levels of precipitation between 2,000mm and 7,000mm a year. This region is marked by steep hills and mountains at the edge of the Central Andes descending into the flat floodplains of the Llanos de Moxos to the north of Cochabamba. Further east of this region is a transition zone between the Tropical Wet-and-Dry forests of Santa Cruz and the Chapare, where Monsoonal climates predominate with an average annual precipitation between 1,800mm and 3,000mm.

South of the Tropical lowlands of Cochabamba lies a thin band of montane cloud forests that run slightly southeast from north to south in Cochabamba. This region features an unusual [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") and [Oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate"), with precipitation year-round, with some drying periods. Precipitation in this region ranges between 1,000mm and 2,500mm.

The center of the department is marked by the temperate xeric valleys of Cochabamba (known as Kanata), Alto Cochabamba, and Capinota. These valley areas are marked by dry montane forests, and semi-arid orographies. Temperate climates year-round feature considerable diurnal temperature variation due to the high altitude. A majority of the department's population lives in this area, where major cities are located like [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), [Cliza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliza_(town) "Cliza (town)"), [Punata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punata "Punata"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo "Quillacollo"), [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani,_Bolivia "Arani, Bolivia"), [Santivańez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiva%C5%84ez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santivańez (page does not exist)"), [Capinota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capinota "Capinota"), [Irpa Irpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irpa_Irpa "Irpa Irpa"), among others.

Surrounding the smaller valleys of the department's center from the west to the east, is a region of Andean highlands, featuring a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate"), with annual precipitation averaging between 400mm and 1,400mm. This region of rocky valleys and moderately sized mountains features mosaics of high altitude forests and agricultural heartland. This region features dramatic and diverse geographies, with a considerable historical and archaeological importance.

To the southeast of the highlands of Cochabamba, are semi-arid valleys and mountains terminating at the banks of the Wapaymayu or Río Grande. This area, famous for its cultural history, is marked by dry valleys and mountains, with agricultural lands bordering rivers throughout the region. Precipitation in this region is generally sparse, oscillating between 300mm and 600mm per year, bordering on a [Desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate "Desert climate")

To the extreme southwest, is a small tract of Puna which features a cold [Tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra_climate "Tundra climate"), with unusual subpolar oceanic characteristics. Precipitation in this area ranges between 300mm and 650mm per year.

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The Cochabamba Assembly has 34 members including two indigenous representatives. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010 and the current composition was determined at the [regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") on 7 March 2021.

The current executive committee, elected on 3 May 2022, consists of Elena Aine Espinoza as president, Francisco Otalora Ticona as first vice-president, Pedro Andrés Badran Leon as second vice-president and Julieta Veizaga Guevara as first secretary.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-9)

### Regions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regions")]

The municipalities in Cochabamba Department can also be grouped informally into large regions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-13) Provinces are not subsumed under regions, which have rather different borders. The five regions are:

*   Región Andina (lit.'Andean Region' or 'Region of the Andes'): the [cordilleras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") in the west, part of the [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano").
*   Cono Sur (lit.'Southern Cone'), a cone-shaped (vaguely triangular) corner in the southeast.
*   [Región Metropolitana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanata_Metropolitan_Area "Kanata Metropolitan Area"): the department's most populous region, centered around the capital city, [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba")
*   Trópico (el Trópico de Cochabamba): the department's largest region, including [Chimoré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimor%C3%A9,_Cochabamba "Chimoré, Cochabamba"), [Colomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colomi "Colomi"), [Entre Rios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entre_Rios,_Cochabamba "Entre Rios, Cochabamba"), [Puerto Villarroel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Villarroel "Puerto Villarroel"), [Shinahota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinahota "Shinahota"), [Villa Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Tunari "Villa Tunari"), and part of the _[llanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos "Llanos") tropicales_
*   Valles (lit.'Valleys'): south of Metropolitana.
