## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

The Cochabamba economy is based mainly in services, but recently it is experiencing some diversification in manufacturing, agriculture and tourism. The geographic location of Cochabamba makes it the main routes of transport joining the two main cities, the host government La Paz and the industrial hub Santa Cruz. Therefore, many cervices i.e. transport, banking, telecommunication, gastronomy, are economically important in the corridor La Paz – Santa Cruz. Extraction of oil was very important for the economy in the past; especially in Chapare where the wells are located. By 2013 many of the exploited wells were showing signs of depletion. Thus, investment is needed to find new productive wells. Once called “the basket grain of Bolivia” today Cochabamba produces just a portion of the agriculture output of the country. Overpopulation in the productive valleys and “minifundio” doomed the once competitive production. Nevertheless, Cochabamba is still important in poultry, dairy, tropical fruits, potatoes, among others. Recently, Cochabamba experiences some improvement in manufacturing and industry. The cement mill of COBOCE located in Capinota almost triples the production tapering the strong demand. The roads to the industrial park and other facilities of the park were improved making it more competitive for the local and new industries. Also, it is worth to mention the almost 1b USD government investment in the petro chemistry (urea plant) located in Bulo Bulo.

**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Quchapampa Jach'a Suyu_, [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Departamento de Cochabamba_ pronounced[[kotʃaˈβamba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/95/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg "File:ES-pe - Cochabamba.ogg"), [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa Suyu_), from Quechua _qucha_ or _qhucha_, meaning "lake", _pampa_ meaning "plain",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-3) is one of the nine departments of Bolivia. It is known to be the [breadbasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadbasket "Breadbasket") of the country because of its variety of agricultural products from its geographical position. It has an area of 55,631 km 2. Its population in the 2024 census was 2,005,373. Its capital is the city of [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), known as the "City of Eternal Spring" and "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Cochabamba valley has been inhabited for over a thousand years due to its fertile productive soils and climate. Archaeological evidence suggests that the initial valley inhabitants were of various ethnic indigenous groups. [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, Omereque and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at various times before the Spanish arrived.

The first Spanish inhabitant of the Valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of Potosí. The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood of the city.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa was founded on 2 August 1571 by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa. It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food for the mining towns of the relatively nearby Altiplano region, particularly the city of Potosí which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 17th century– funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power at the time. With the silver mining industry in Potosi at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries of existence. The city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786, King Charles III of Spain renamed the city to the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in Oruro by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 mestizos, 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 mulattos and 175 African slaves.

In 2000, Cochabamba was wracked by large-scale protests over the privatisation of the city's water supply, known as the [Water War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Water_War "Cochabamba Water War").

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured. The democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, a former military aide to the Luis García Meza dictatorship of the 1980s, had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's eastern departments in a dispute with President Evo Morales over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions have not been resolved.

In July 2007, a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.

In August 2008, a nationwide referendum was held, and while President Evo Morales had 67% support in Bolivia, the Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters of the department.

In 2018 Cochabamba hosted the 2018 South American Games ODESUR.

Around 74% of Cochabambinos identify as indigenous, while most of the remaining population is mestizo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Cochabamba Department is bordered by [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department") and Potosi Departments to the south, [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department") and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") Departments to the west, Beni Department to the north, and [Santa Cruz Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the east. The borders are formed mainly by rivers, like **Ichilo** to the east, **Rio Grande** to the south and **Cotacajes** to the west.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-5)

[![Image 9: Map of Cochabamba showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Cochabamba, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Geographically and climatically, Cochabamba is one of Bolivia's most diverse regions, with a similar orography and diversity to [La Paz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)"). Cochabamba is made up of a variety of regions. The northern portions of the department, known as the Chapare, is a region of moist [Southwestern Amazonian moist forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Amazonian_moist_forests "Southwestern Amazonian moist forests") with high levels of precipitation between 2,000mm and 7,000mm a year. This region is marked by steep hills and mountains at the edge of the Central Andes descending into the flat floodplains of the Llanos de Moxos to the north of Cochabamba. Further east of this region is a transition zone between the Tropical Wet-and-Dry forests of Santa Cruz and the Chapare, where Monsoonal climates predominate with an average annual precipitation between 1,800mm and 3,000mm.

South of the Tropical lowlands of Cochabamba lies a thin band of montane cloud forests that run slightly southeast from north to south in Cochabamba. This region features an unusual [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") and [Oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate"), with precipitation year-round, with some drying periods. Precipitation in this region ranges between 1,000mm and 2,500mm.

The center of the department is marked by the temperate xeric valleys of Cochabamba (known as Kanata), Alto Cochabamba, and Capinota. These valley areas are marked by dry montane forests, and semi-arid orographies. Temperate climates year-round feature considerable diurnal temperature variation due to the high altitude. A majority of the department's population lives in this area, where major cities are located like [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), [Cliza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliza_(town) "Cliza (town)"), [Punata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punata "Punata"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo "Quillacollo"), [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani,_Bolivia "Arani, Bolivia"), [Santivańez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiva%C5%84ez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santivańez (page does not exist)"), [Capinota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capinota "Capinota"), [Irpa Irpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irpa_Irpa "Irpa Irpa"), among others.

Surrounding the smaller valleys of the department's center from the west to the east, is a region of Andean highlands, featuring a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate"), with annual precipitation averaging between 400mm and 1,400mm. This region of rocky valleys and moderately sized mountains features mosaics of high altitude forests and agricultural heartland. This region features dramatic and diverse geographies, with a considerable historical and archaeological importance.

To the southeast of the highlands of Cochabamba, are semi-arid valleys and mountains terminating at the banks of the Wapaymayu or Río Grande. This area, famous for its cultural history, is marked by dry valleys and mountains, with agricultural lands bordering rivers throughout the region. Precipitation in this region is generally sparse, oscillating between 300mm and 600mm per year, bordering on a [Desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate "Desert climate")

To the extreme southwest, is a small tract of Puna which features a cold [Tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra_climate "Tundra climate"), with unusual subpolar oceanic characteristics. Precipitation in this area ranges between 300mm and 650mm per year.

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

Since May 2010, the chief executive officer of Bolivia departments has been the governor; before then, the officer was called the prefect, and until 2006, the prefect was appointed by the [president of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). The current governor, Humberto Sánchez of the [Movement for Socialism– Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") (MAS–IPSP) was elected on 7 March 2021 and took office on 4 May.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-6)

The MAS–IPSP has been the dominant political party in the department since the 2008 recall referendum.

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The Cochabamba Assembly has 34 members including two indigenous representatives. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010 and the current composition was determined at the [regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") on 7 March 2021.

The current executive committee, elected on 3 May 2022, consists of Elena Aine Espinoza as president, Francisco Otalora Ticona as first vice-president, Pedro Andrés Badran Leon as second vice-president and Julieta Veizaga Guevara as first secretary.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-9)

### Regions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regions")]

The municipalities in Cochabamba Department can also be grouped informally into large regions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-13) Provinces are not subsumed under regions, which have rather different borders. The five regions are:

*   Región Andina (lit.'Andean Region' or 'Region of the Andes'): the [cordilleras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") in the west, part of the [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano").
*   Cono Sur (lit.'Southern Cone'), a cone-shaped (vaguely triangular) corner in the southeast.
*   [Región Metropolitana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanata_Metropolitan_Area "Kanata Metropolitan Area"): the department's most populous region, centered around the capital city, [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba")
*   Trópico (el Trópico de Cochabamba): the department's largest region, including [Chimoré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimor%C3%A9,_Cochabamba "Chimoré, Cochabamba"), [Colomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colomi "Colomi"), [Entre Rios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entre_Rios,_Cochabamba "Entre Rios, Cochabamba"), [Puerto Villarroel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Villarroel "Puerto Villarroel"), [Shinahota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinahota "Shinahota"), [Villa Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Tunari "Villa Tunari"), and part of the _[llanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos "Llanos") tropicales_
*   Valles (lit.'Valleys'): south of Metropolitana.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

The Cochabamba economy is based mainly in services, but recently it is experiencing some diversification in manufacturing, agriculture and tourism. The geographic location of Cochabamba makes it the main routes of transport joining the two main cities, the host government La Paz and the industrial hub Santa Cruz. Therefore, many cervices i.e. transport, banking, telecommunication, gastronomy, are economically important in the corridor La Paz – Santa Cruz. Extraction of oil was very important for the economy in the past; especially in Chapare where the wells are located. By 2013 many of the exploited wells were showing signs of depletion. Thus, investment is needed to find new productive wells. Once called “the basket grain of Bolivia” today Cochabamba produces just a portion of the agriculture output of the country. Overpopulation in the productive valleys and “minifundio” doomed the once competitive production. Nevertheless, Cochabamba is still important in poultry, dairy, tropical fruits, potatoes, among others. Recently, Cochabamba experiences some improvement in manufacturing and industry. The cement mill of COBOCE located in Capinota almost triples the production tapering the strong demand. The roads to the industrial park and other facilities of the park were improved making it more competitive for the local and new industries. Also, it is worth to mention the almost 1b USD government investment in the petro chemistry (urea plant) located in Bulo Bulo.

The **departments** of [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_), informally called **regions** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _regiones_), are the first-level [administrative subdivisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_subdivisions "Administrative subdivisions") of the country. According to the _Organic Law of Regional Governments_, each department is administered by a [regional government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_governments_of_Peru "Regional governments of Peru") and a legislature responsible for administration, economic planning, and public services. These governments operate with autonomy while still coordinating with national authorities. Each department is led by a regional governor, who is elected by popular vote for a four-year term, and is responsible for implementing regional policies, managing budgets, and overseeing infrastructure projects. The governor is supported by a regional legislative council, composed of elected representatives from different provinces within the department. This council approves budgets, monitors public investments, and ensures government accountability.

There are 24 departments in total, as well as two [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru") that operate under a special regime: [Callao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callao "Callao") and [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_province "Lima province"). The former does not belong to any department since 1836, but is nevertheless administered by a [regional government of its own](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Government_of_Callao "Regional Government of Callao"). The latter is administered by the [Metropolitan Municipality of Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Municipality_of_Lima "Metropolitan Municipality of Lima"), which is equal in status to a regional government.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-2)

Each department is further divided into [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru"), which are governed by [provincial municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Peru "Municipalities of Peru"). These municipalities are led by a mayor and a council, also elected by the population. They manage local services such as urban planning, transportation, and sanitation. Within the provinces, there are [district municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Peru "Municipalities of Peru"), responsible for more localized governance, including community development, minor public works, and social programs. This three-tiered structure—regional, provincial, and district—ensures that governance reaches all levels, from large cities to rural villages.

Although the departments have autonomy, they still follow national laws and policies set by the central government. The **National Decentralized Secretariat** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Secretaría de Descentralización_), under the [Presidency of the Council of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Peru "Prime Minister of Peru"), oversees regional governments to ensure efficiency and compliance. Departments also coordinate with [national ministries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministries_of_Peru "List of ministries of Peru") for education, health, transportation, and security, receiving funding and technical support. This structure allows departments to manage their own affairs while maintaining a connection to the broader national development strategy.

As political and economic power increasingly concentrated in Lima, the capital city, several administrations attempted to decentralize the country with little success.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-27) The 1979 [Peruvian Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Constitution "Peruvian Constitution") contained provisions for the decentralization of power through the creation of autonomous regions, but they were not implemented.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-28)

During the later years of the 1985–1990 presidency of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García"), the government faced the prospect of losing the 1990 presidential elections because of a widespread economic crisis and faltering public support. As a way of creating an alternative source of power, the regime established twelve autonomous regions on January 20, 1989, in the hope of winning some elections at this level.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-29) However, due to the haste of their creation, these regional governments were not provided with fiscal resources of their own, so they depended on the goodwill of the central government for funding.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-30) Formation of another region was delayed by the reluctance of the [Constitutional Province of Callao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callao "Callao") to merge with the [Lima Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_Department "Lima Department"). Originally San Martín and La Libertad Regions formed the sole region of _San Martín-La Libertad_ but later were split.

### Later history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regions_of_Peru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later history")]

The [1990 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Peruvian_general_election "1990 Peruvian general election") were marked by the discrediting of political parties as evidenced in the election of [Alberto Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Fujimori "Alberto Fujimori"), an independent candidate. Fujimori withheld financial transfers to regional governments and then, on December 29, 1992, replaced them with government-designated Transitory Councils of Regional Administration ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Consejos Transitorios de Administración Regional_). Having dissolved Congress in the [1992 Peruvian constitutional crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Peruvian_constitutional_crisis "1992 Peruvian constitutional crisis"), Fujimori called an election for a Constitutional Assembly which drafted the [1993 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Constitution "Peruvian Constitution"). This new text included provisions for the creation of regions with autonomous, elected governments, but they were not carried out. A framework law on decentralization ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley Marco de Descentralización_) issued on January 30, 1998, confirmed the permanence of transitory councils, now under the supervision of the [Ministry of the Presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Presidency_(Peru) "Ministry of the Presidency (Peru)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-33)

Fujimori was forced to resign in November 2000 under accusations of authoritarianism, corruption, and human rights violations.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-34) After an interim government led by [Valentín Paniagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valent%C3%ADn_Paniagua "Valentín Paniagua"), [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo") was elected president for the 2001–2006 period on a platform that included creating regional governments.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-35) The new administration laid out the legal framework for the new administrative subdivisions in the Decentralization Bases Law ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley de Bases de la Descentralización_), issued on July 17, 2002, and the Organic Law of Regional Governments ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley Orgánica de Gobiernos Regionales_) issued on November 19, 2002. New regional governments were elected on November 20, 2002, one in each of the former departments and the former Constitutional Province ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Provincia Constitucional_) of Callao. The [province of Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Lima "Province of Lima"), containing the capital, was excluded from the process; thus, it is not part of any region.

In the 2002 elections, most regional governments went to parties in opposition, with twelve going to the [APRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alianza_Popular_Revolucionaria_Americana "Alianza Popular Revolucionaria Americana") of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García") and only one each to [Possible Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possible_Peru "Possible Peru"), the party of president [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo") and ally [Independent Moralizing Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Moralizing_Front "Independent Moralizing Front") of [Fernando Olivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Olivera_(politician) "Fernando Olivera (politician)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-36) The combination of a strong opposition and a weak government led to concerns about an impending political crisis. However, this did not turn out to be the case as the new regional governments were absorbed by local problems and showed little initiative in national politics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-37) As the territorial circumscriptions that regional governments inherited from the former departments are considered too small, the Decentralization Bases Law provides for mergers between departments after a majority of the populations involved express their approval up to become a formal region.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-38) The first referendum of this kind was carried out on October 30, 2005, with the following proposals being put to the ballot:

*   [Apurímac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apur%C3%ADmac_Region "Apurímac Region"), [Cuzco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuzco_Region "Cuzco Region")
*   [Arequipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arequipa_Region "Arequipa Region"), [Puno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puno_Region "Puno Region"), [Tacna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacna_Region "Tacna Region")
*   [Ayacucho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayacucho_Region "Ayacucho Region"), [Huancavelica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huancavelica_Region "Huancavelica Region"), [Ica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ica_Region "Ica Region")
*   [Ancash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancash_Region "Ancash Region"), [Huánuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu%C3%A1nuco_Region "Huánuco Region"), [Junín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun%C3%ADn_Region "Junín Region"), [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_Region "Lima Region"), [Pasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasco_Region "Pasco Region")
*   [Lambayeque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambayeque_Region "Lambayeque Region"), [Piura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piura_Region "Piura Region"), [Tumbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumbes_Region "Tumbes Region")

These proposals were rejected by the electorate of all departments involved except for Arequipa. Thus, no merger was carried out.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-39)

New elections for regional governments were held on November 19, 2006; most regions went to local political movements rather than to national parties. The APRA, which had won the presidential elections held on June 4, 2006, only won in two regions, all other national parties achieved even less.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-40)

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regions_of_Peru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Government")]

Main article: [Regional Governments of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Governments_of_Peru "Regional Governments of Peru")

According to the Organic Law of Regional Governments, the responsibilities of regional governments include planning regional development, executing public investment projects, promoting economic activities, and managing public property.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-41) Regional governments are composed of a president and a council, elected for a four-year term; additionally, there is a coordination council integrated by [provincial mayors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru") and representatives of the [civil society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_society "Civil society").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-42) The Regional President is the [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government "Head of government"); his functions include proposing and enforcing the budget, appointing government officials, issuing decrees and resolutions, executing regional plans and programs, and administering regional properties and rents.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-43) The Regional Council debates and votes upon bills proposed by the regional president, it also oversees all regional officials and can remove the president, its vice president, and any council member from office.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-44) The Regional Coordination Council has a consultancy role in planning and budget issues, and it has no executive or legislative powers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-45)

The Organic Law of Regional Governments stipulates the gradual transfer of functions from the central government to the regions, provided they are certified as capable of undertaking these tasks.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-46) To oversee this process, the Decentralization Bases Law created a National Council of Decentralization ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Consejo Nacional de Descentralización_).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-47) However, this institution was criticized for being bureaucratic and ineffective by the government of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García"), former president of Peru. Thus, on January 24, 2007, the council was abolished and replaced by the Decentralization Secretariat ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Secretaría de Descentralización_), a dependency of the [Prime Minister office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Peru "Prime Minister of Peru").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-48) Two months later, the regional presidents gathered in the city of [Huánuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu%C3%A1nuco "Huánuco") established a [National Assembly of Regional Governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Regional_Governments "National Assembly of Regional Governments") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Asamblea Nacional de Gobiernos Regionales_) as an alternative coordinating institution, independent from the Central Government.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-49)

The **departments** of [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_), informally called **regions** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _regiones_), are the first-level [administrative subdivisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_subdivisions "Administrative subdivisions") of the country. According to the _Organic Law of Regional Governments_, each department is administered by a [regional government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_governments_of_Peru "Regional governments of Peru") and a legislature responsible for administration, economic planning, and public services. These governments operate with autonomy while still coordinating with national authorities. Each department is led by a regional governor, who is elected by popular vote for a four-year term, and is responsible for implementing regional policies, managing budgets, and overseeing infrastructure projects. The governor is supported by a regional legislative council, composed of elected representatives from different provinces within the department. This council approves budgets, monitors public investments, and ensures government accountability.

There are 24 departments in total, as well as two [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru") that operate under a special regime: [Callao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callao "Callao") and [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_province "Lima province"). The former does not belong to any department since 1836, but is nevertheless administered by a [regional government of its own](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Government_of_Callao "Regional Government of Callao"). The latter is administered by the [Metropolitan Municipality of Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Municipality_of_Lima "Metropolitan Municipality of Lima"), which is equal in status to a regional government.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-2)

Each department is further divided into [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru"), which are governed by [provincial municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Peru "Municipalities of Peru"). These municipalities are led by a mayor and a council, also elected by the population. They manage local services such as urban planning, transportation, and sanitation. Within the provinces, there are [district municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Peru "Municipalities of Peru"), responsible for more localized governance, including community development, minor public works, and social programs. This three-tiered structure—regional, provincial, and district—ensures that governance reaches all levels, from large cities to rural villages.

Although the departments have autonomy, they still follow national laws and policies set by the central government. The **National Decentralized Secretariat** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Secretaría de Descentralización_), under the [Presidency of the Council of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Peru "Prime Minister of Peru"), oversees regional governments to ensure efficiency and compliance. Departments also coordinate with [national ministries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministries_of_Peru "List of ministries of Peru") for education, health, transportation, and security, receiving funding and technical support. This structure allows departments to manage their own affairs while maintaining a connection to the broader national development strategy.

*   [Tacna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Tacna "Department of Tacna")[[v]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-24)
*   [Tumbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Tumbes "Department of Tumbes")[[w]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-25)
*   [Ucayali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Ucayali "Department of Ucayali")[[x]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-26)

As political and economic power increasingly concentrated in Lima, the capital city, several administrations attempted to decentralize the country with little success.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-27) The 1979 [Peruvian Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Constitution "Peruvian Constitution") contained provisions for the decentralization of power through the creation of autonomous regions, but they were not implemented.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-28)

During the later years of the 1985–1990 presidency of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García"), the government faced the prospect of losing the 1990 presidential elections because of a widespread economic crisis and faltering public support. As a way of creating an alternative source of power, the regime established twelve autonomous regions on January 20, 1989, in the hope of winning some elections at this level.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-29) However, due to the haste of their creation, these regional governments were not provided with fiscal resources of their own, so they depended on the goodwill of the central government for funding.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-30) Formation of another region was delayed by the reluctance of the [Constitutional Province of Callao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callao "Callao") to merge with the [Lima Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_Department "Lima Department"). Originally San Martín and La Libertad Regions formed the sole region of _San Martín-La Libertad_ but later were split.

### Later history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regions_of_Peru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later history")]

The [1990 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Peruvian_general_election "1990 Peruvian general election") were marked by the discrediting of political parties as evidenced in the election of [Alberto Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Fujimori "Alberto Fujimori"), an independent candidate. Fujimori withheld financial transfers to regional governments and then, on December 29, 1992, replaced them with government-designated Transitory Councils of Regional Administration ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Consejos Transitorios de Administración Regional_). Having dissolved Congress in the [1992 Peruvian constitutional crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Peruvian_constitutional_crisis "1992 Peruvian constitutional crisis"), Fujimori called an election for a Constitutional Assembly which drafted the [1993 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Constitution "Peruvian Constitution"). This new text included provisions for the creation of regions with autonomous, elected governments, but they were not carried out. A framework law on decentralization ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley Marco de Descentralización_) issued on January 30, 1998, confirmed the permanence of transitory councils, now under the supervision of the [Ministry of the Presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Presidency_(Peru) "Ministry of the Presidency (Peru)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-33)

Fujimori was forced to resign in November 2000 under accusations of authoritarianism, corruption, and human rights violations.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-34) After an interim government led by [Valentín Paniagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valent%C3%ADn_Paniagua "Valentín Paniagua"), [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo") was elected president for the 2001–2006 period on a platform that included creating regional governments.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-35) The new administration laid out the legal framework for the new administrative subdivisions in the Decentralization Bases Law ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley de Bases de la Descentralización_), issued on July 17, 2002, and the Organic Law of Regional Governments ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Ley Orgánica de Gobiernos Regionales_) issued on November 19, 2002. New regional governments were elected on November 20, 2002, one in each of the former departments and the former Constitutional Province ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Provincia Constitucional_) of Callao. The [province of Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Lima "Province of Lima"), containing the capital, was excluded from the process; thus, it is not part of any region.

In the 2002 elections, most regional governments went to parties in opposition, with twelve going to the [APRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alianza_Popular_Revolucionaria_Americana "Alianza Popular Revolucionaria Americana") of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García") and only one each to [Possible Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possible_Peru "Possible Peru"), the party of president [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo") and ally [Independent Moralizing Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Moralizing_Front "Independent Moralizing Front") of [Fernando Olivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Olivera_(politician) "Fernando Olivera (politician)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-36) The combination of a strong opposition and a weak government led to concerns about an impending political crisis. However, this did not turn out to be the case as the new regional governments were absorbed by local problems and showed little initiative in national politics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-37) As the territorial circumscriptions that regional governments inherited from the former departments are considered too small, the Decentralization Bases Law provides for mergers between departments after a majority of the populations involved express their approval up to become a formal region.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-38) The first referendum of this kind was carried out on October 30, 2005, with the following proposals being put to the ballot:

*   [Apurímac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apur%C3%ADmac_Region "Apurímac Region"), [Cuzco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuzco_Region "Cuzco Region")
*   [Arequipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arequipa_Region "Arequipa Region"), [Puno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puno_Region "Puno Region"), [Tacna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacna_Region "Tacna Region")
*   [Ayacucho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayacucho_Region "Ayacucho Region"), [Huancavelica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huancavelica_Region "Huancavelica Region"), [Ica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ica_Region "Ica Region")
*   [Ancash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancash_Region "Ancash Region"), [Huánuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu%C3%A1nuco_Region "Huánuco Region"), [Junín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun%C3%ADn_Region "Junín Region"), [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_Region "Lima Region"), [Pasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasco_Region "Pasco Region")
*   [Lambayeque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambayeque_Region "Lambayeque Region"), [Piura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piura_Region "Piura Region"), [Tumbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumbes_Region "Tumbes Region")

These proposals were rejected by the electorate of all departments involved except for Arequipa. Thus, no merger was carried out.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-39)

New elections for regional governments were held on November 19, 2006; most regions went to local political movements rather than to national parties. The APRA, which had won the presidential elections held on June 4, 2006, only won in two regions, all other national parties achieved even less.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-40)

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regions_of_Peru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Government")]

Main article: [Regional Governments of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Governments_of_Peru "Regional Governments of Peru")

According to the Organic Law of Regional Governments, the responsibilities of regional governments include planning regional development, executing public investment projects, promoting economic activities, and managing public property.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-41) Regional governments are composed of a president and a council, elected for a four-year term; additionally, there is a coordination council integrated by [provincial mayors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Peru "Provinces of Peru") and representatives of the [civil society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_society "Civil society").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-42) The Regional President is the [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government "Head of government"); his functions include proposing and enforcing the budget, appointing government officials, issuing decrees and resolutions, executing regional plans and programs, and administering regional properties and rents.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-43) The Regional Council debates and votes upon bills proposed by the regional president, it also oversees all regional officials and can remove the president, its vice president, and any council member from office.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-44) The Regional Coordination Council has a consultancy role in planning and budget issues, and it has no executive or legislative powers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-45)

The Organic Law of Regional Governments stipulates the gradual transfer of functions from the central government to the regions, provided they are certified as capable of undertaking these tasks.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-46) To oversee this process, the Decentralization Bases Law created a National Council of Decentralization ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Consejo Nacional de Descentralización_).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-47) However, this institution was criticized for being bureaucratic and ineffective by the government of [Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García"), former president of Peru. Thus, on January 24, 2007, the council was abolished and replaced by the Decentralization Secretariat ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Secretaría de Descentralización_), a dependency of the [Prime Minister office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Peru "Prime Minister of Peru").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-48) Two months later, the regional presidents gathered in the city of [Huánuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu%C3%A1nuco "Huánuco") established a [National Assembly of Regional Governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Regional_Governments "National Assembly of Regional Governments") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Asamblea Nacional de Gobiernos Regionales_) as an alternative coordinating institution, independent from the Central Government.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Peru#cite_note-49)

**Antioquia** (Spanish pronunciation:[[anˈtjokja]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/4d/ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg/ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg "File:ES-pe - Antioquia.ogg")) is one of the 32 [departments of Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Colombia "Departments of Colombia"), located in the central northwestern part of Colombia with a narrow section that borders the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"). Most of its territory is [mountainous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountainous "Mountainous") with some [valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley "Valley"), much of which is part of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range. Antioquia has been part of many territorial divisions of former countries created within the present-day territory of Colombia. Before the adoption of the [Colombian Constitution of 1886](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_Constitution_of_1886 "Colombian Constitution of 1886"), [Antioquia State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_State "Antioquia State") had a sovereign government.

The department covers an area of 63,612 km 2 (24,561 sq mi), and has a population of 6,994,792 (2023). Antioquia borders the [Córdoba department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba_department "Córdoba department") and the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") to the north; [Chocó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_department "Chocó department") to the west; the departments of [Bolívar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol%C3%ADvar_department "Bolívar department"), [Santander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santander_department "Santander department"), and [Boyaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyac%C3%A1_department "Boyacá department") to the east; and the departments of [Caldas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldas_Department "Caldas Department") and [Risaralda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risaralda_Department "Risaralda Department") to the south.

[Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín") is Antioquia's capital and the second-largest city in the country. Other important towns are [Rionegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rionegro "Rionegro") located in the [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Antioquia "Eastern Antioquia"), [Apartadó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartad%C3%B3 "Apartadó") on the [Caribbean Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_region_of_Colombia "Caribbean region of Colombia"), [Santa Fe de Antioquia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_de_Antioquia "Santa Fe de Antioquia"), the old capital on the [Cauca River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauca_River "Cauca River"), and [Puerto Berrío](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Berr%C3%ADo "Puerto Berrío") on the [Magdalena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_River "Magdalena River").

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg/250px-Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg)

[Guatapé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatap%C3%A9 "Guatapé") reservoir

Antioquia is the [sixth-largest department of Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Colombian_departments_by_area "List of Colombian departments by area"). It is predominantly mountainous, crossed by the [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") and the [Cordillera Occidental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Occidental_(Colombia) "Cordillera Occidental (Colombia)") of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes"). The [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") divides to form the [Aburrá valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aburr%C3%A1_Valley "Aburrá Valley"), in which the capital, [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"), is located. The [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") forms the plateaus of [Santa Rosa de Osos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Rosa_de_Osos "Santa Rosa de Osos") and [Rionegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rionegro,_Antioquia "Rionegro, Antioquia").

While 80% of the department's territory is mountainous, Antioquia also has lowlands in [Bajo Cauca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bajo_Cauca "Bajo Cauca"), [Magdalena Medio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_Medio_Antioquia "Magdalena Medio Antioquia"), and eastern [Sonsón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons%C3%B3n "Sonsón"), as well as coastline on the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"), in [Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-6) This area has a tropical climate and is of high strategic importance due to its location.

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg/250px-Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg)

[La Ceja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ceja,_Antioquia "La Ceja, Antioquia")

The basis for the name Antioquia is uncertain. A common explanation is that it was named after the [Hellenistic-founded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_Greece "Hellenistic Greece") city in [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria_(region) "Syria (region)") of [Antioch on the Orontes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch_on_the_Orontes "Antioch on the Orontes") ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Ἀντιόχεια _Antiocheia_, [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic"): _Antāqiyyah_, now officially [Antakya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antakya "Antakya"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey")). The region of Colombia known as the Coffee Zone has a strong influence from [Arab Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Jews "Arab Jews"), both demographically and culturally, and many towns and cities are named after cities in the Middle East. Moreover, ancient Antioch played a significant role in developing the communities of [early Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Christianity "Early Christianity") and thus was important to the Catholic Spaniard conquistadors.

There are many other cities in the Middle East named [Antiochia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochia_(disambiguation) "Antiochia (disambiguation)"), which were likewise named for the [Antiochid rulers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochus_(disambiguation)#The_Seleucid_Empire "Antiochus (disambiguation)") during the [Seleucid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seleucid_Empire "Seleucid Empire") (312–63 BC).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

### Native people of Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Native people of Antioquia")]

See also: [Columbian exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange "Columbian exchange")

Before Spanish colonization, [Indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_South_America "Indigenous peoples of South America") inhabited the Antioquia region. Some specialists believe they came from [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"), while others say they came from the interior [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River").

Antioquia was primarily populated by the [Kalina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalina_people "Kalina people") or "Mainland Caribs." Some scattered groups of [Muisca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muisca "Muisca") were said to be present in the [Darién](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dari%C3%A9n_Province "Darién Province") region, a coastal region in the far north that is now in [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), but no historical records refer to Muisca in Antioquia.

The Kalina in Antioquia comprised smaller groups called families. The most prominent were the Catía, [Nutabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutabe "Nutabe"), and [Tahamí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taham%C3%AD_people "Tahamí people"), who inhabited central Antioquia. The [Quimbaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimbaya "Quimbaya") occupied southern Antioquia.

The Quimbaya, Kalina, and Muisca were the most prominent groups the [conquistadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador") encountered upon their arrival in Antioquia.

The Spaniards had a turbulent history of encounters with the Carib. Although the tribe was numerous and known for its warring culture, the Spaniards dominated or exterminated them in the process of [conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_(military) "Conquest (military)") and [colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization "Colonization"). Like all [indigenous peoples of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), many died in [virgin soil epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_soil_epidemic "Virgin soil epidemic") of diseases endemic to Eurasia.

Some surviving natives dispersed to evade the Spanish, and some committed suicide to escape [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery"). Many survivors fled to what is now [Chocó department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_department "Chocó department"). Barely 0.5% of Antioquia's population is Indigenous, but most residents have a significant Indigenous genetic component (26% on average).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-7)

### Basque and Jewish influence in Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Basque and Jewish influence in Antioquia")]

[Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")'s [Basque Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_Country_(greater_region) "Basque Country (greater region)") and [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") have influenced Antioquia and its language since the Spanish colonization. This began in 1499 during the [third voyage of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus "Voyages of Christopher Columbus"). The owner and master of the _[Santa María](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_Mar%C3%ADa\_(ship) "Santa María (ship)")_, second in command to Columbus, was [Juan de la Cosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_la_Cosa "Juan de la Cosa"), nicknamed _el Vizcaino_ ("the [Biscayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscay "Biscay")"). Hundreds of [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basques "Basques") settled in the area, sponsored by the Spanish colonization companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-9)

#### Dialect

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dialect")]

Immigrants influenced the Spanish spoken in Antioquia in several ways:

*   Immigrants from [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia") and the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands") brought their preference for _[seseo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seseo "Seseo")_, a uniform pronunciation of "s", "z", and soft "c".
*   However, those from [Extremadura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremadura "Extremadura") favored an [apico-alveolar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolar_fricative#Voiceless_apico-alveolar_sibilant "Voiceless alveolar fricative") sound (part way to "sh").
*   The [digraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") "ll" (double L) is [affricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affricate "Affricate"), like English "j".
*   Certain words beginning with "r" are [prefixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epenthesis "Epenthesis") by "a" (with the "r" doubled to continue to indicate that it is trilled): 
    *   _arrecostarse_ instead of _recostarse_
    *   _arrecoger_ instead of _recoger_
    *   _arrecordarse_ instead of _recordarse_.

*   Specific words have been adopted, such as _coscorria_ (useless, inept) and _tap_ (tap).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-10)

#### Local character

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Local character")]

It has been asserted since the mid-nineteenth century that Basque and Jewish origins have influenced the character of Antioquia. Specific evidence of cultural contribution is sparse, perhaps partly because Basque is not dominant in Spain.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-11) However, American historian Everett Hagen sampled the Medellín telephone directory in 1957 and found that 15% of the surnames were of Basque origin, but 25% of the employers were. He concluded that Basque influence was important in explaining the increased industrial development of Antioquia in Colombia. The study reinforced notions of the character of social groups, though it has been criticized as stereotypical.

### Spaniards in Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Spaniards in Antioquia")]

The first Spaniard known to have visited the territory now known as Antioquia was [Rodrigo de Bastidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_de_Bastidas "Rodrigo de Bastidas"), who explored the area around the future site of [Darién](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dari%C3%A9n_Province "Darién Province") in 1500. Ten years later, [Alonso de Ojeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_de_Ojeda "Alonso de Ojeda") founded [San Sebastián de Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n_de_Urab%C3%A1 "San Sebastián de Urabá"), 2 km from the present-day town of [Necoclí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necocl%C3%AD "Necoclí"). It was later destroyed by the natives. The first Spanish military incursion into Antioquia, however, was not made until 1537. An expedition commanded by [Francisco César](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_C%C3%A9sar "Francisco César") traveled through the lands of chief Dabeiba, arriving at the [Cauca River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauca_River "Cauca River"). They were said to have taken important treasures from the indigenous people's tombs. In response, the warriors of chief Nutibara harassed the Spaniards continually, and forced them to return to [Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia").

In 1541, the conquistador [Jorge Robledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Robledo_(conquistador) "Jorge Robledo (conquistador)") departed from the site of the future (1542) Spanish town of Arma, a little below Aguadas in the North of Caldas, to lead an expedition north on the Cauca River.

Farther north, Robledo would found the city of [Santa Fe de Antioquia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_de_Antioquia "Santa Fe de Antioquia"), which in 1813 was declared the capital of the sovereign and independent state of Antioquia, and remained the seat of the governate until 1826, when Medellín was designated the capital.

### 16th to the 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 16th to the 21st centuries")]

Due to its geographical isolation, being located among mountains, Antioquia suffered supply problems. Its topography did not allow for much agriculture, so the city became dependent upon trade, especially of gold and gin for the colonization of new land. Much of this trade was due to reforms passed after a 1785 visit from [Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Antonio_Mon_y_Velarde?action=edit&redlink=1 "Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde (page does not exist)"), an inspector of the Spanish Crown. The Antioquia became colonizers and traders.

The department was hard hit by the [Colombian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_conflict "Colombian conflict"), with 30,000 people missing between 1997 and 2005.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-12)

_[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ and Citi announced in the year 2013 that [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"), the capital of the department of Antioquia, is the winner of the City of the Year competition, a global program developed in partnership with the [Urban Land Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Land_Institute "Urban Land Institute") to recognize the most innovative urban centers. Medellín was ranked above the other finalists, [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv") and [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-14)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The population of Antioquia is 6,994,792 (2023), of which more than half live in the metropolitan area of [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"). The racial composition is:[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-17)

*   [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people "White people") / [Mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") (88.6%)
*   [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people") or [Afro-Colombian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombians "Colombians") (10.9%)
*   [Indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_in_Colombia "Indigenous peoples in Colombia") or [Amerindian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amerindian "Amerindian") (0.5%)

During the 16th and 18th centuries, Antioquia received many immigrants from Spain, especially [northern Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Spain "Northern Spain").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-19) Most Indigenous peoples died from the introduction of European diseases, and many of those who survived intermarried with early Spanish settlers, who were mostly men; later, Spanish women also began to immigrate. Thousands of Scottish and English who settled in Antioquia fought for the Colombian army during independence.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-20) During the 19th and 20th centuries, immigrants (including Jews)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-21) arrived from Italy, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Portugal, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine and Syria.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-24) Many people from Antioquia are referred to as [Paisas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paisa_Region "Paisa Region"), people of mainly Spanish ancestry, a lot of them Basque.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-25) There is a small Afro-Colombian and Zambo-Colombian (people of Indigenous and African descent) population originating in the majority of the [Urabá subregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia") and the neighboring departments of [Chocó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_Department "Chocó Department"), [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba_Department "Córdoba Department") and [Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre_Department "Sucre Department").
