**Antioquia** (Spanish pronunciation:[[anˈtjokja]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/4d/ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg/ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Antioquia.ogg "File:ES-pe - Antioquia.ogg")) is one of the 32 [departments of Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Colombia "Departments of Colombia"), located in the central northwestern part of Colombia with a narrow section that borders the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"). Most of its territory is [mountainous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountainous "Mountainous") with some [valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley "Valley"), much of which is part of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range. Antioquia has been part of many territorial divisions of former countries created within the present-day territory of Colombia. Before the adoption of the [Colombian Constitution of 1886](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_Constitution_of_1886 "Colombian Constitution of 1886"), [Antioquia State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_State "Antioquia State") had a sovereign government.

The department covers an area of 63,612 km 2 (24,561 sq mi), and has a population of 6,994,792 (2023). Antioquia borders the [Córdoba department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba_department "Córdoba department") and the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") to the north; [Chocó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_department "Chocó department") to the west; the departments of [Bolívar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol%C3%ADvar_department "Bolívar department"), [Santander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santander_department "Santander department"), and [Boyaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyac%C3%A1_department "Boyacá department") to the east; and the departments of [Caldas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldas_Department "Caldas Department") and [Risaralda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risaralda_Department "Risaralda Department") to the south.

[Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín") is Antioquia's capital and the second-largest city in the country. Other important towns are [Rionegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rionegro "Rionegro") located in the [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Antioquia "Eastern Antioquia"), [Apartadó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartad%C3%B3 "Apartadó") on the [Caribbean Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_region_of_Colombia "Caribbean region of Colombia"), [Santa Fe de Antioquia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_de_Antioquia "Santa Fe de Antioquia"), the old capital on the [Cauca River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauca_River "Cauca River"), and [Puerto Berrío](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Berr%C3%ADo "Puerto Berrío") on the [Magdalena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_River "Magdalena River").

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg/250px-Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guatap%C3%A9_Colombia.jpg)

[Guatapé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatap%C3%A9 "Guatapé") reservoir

Antioquia is the [sixth-largest department of Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Colombian_departments_by_area "List of Colombian departments by area"). It is predominantly mountainous, crossed by the [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") and the [Cordillera Occidental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Occidental_(Colombia) "Cordillera Occidental (Colombia)") of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes"). The [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") divides to form the [Aburrá valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aburr%C3%A1_Valley "Aburrá Valley"), in which the capital, [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"), is located. The [Cordillera Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") forms the plateaus of [Santa Rosa de Osos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Rosa_de_Osos "Santa Rosa de Osos") and [Rionegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rionegro,_Antioquia "Rionegro, Antioquia").

While 80% of the department's territory is mountainous, Antioquia also has lowlands in [Bajo Cauca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bajo_Cauca "Bajo Cauca"), [Magdalena Medio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_Medio_Antioquia "Magdalena Medio Antioquia"), and eastern [Sonsón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons%C3%B3n "Sonsón"), as well as coastline on the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"), in [Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-6) This area has a tropical climate and is of high strategic importance due to its location.

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg/250px-Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Panor%C3%A1mica_de_La_Ceja.jpg)

[La Ceja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ceja,_Antioquia "La Ceja, Antioquia")

The basis for the name Antioquia is uncertain. A common explanation is that it was named after the [Hellenistic-founded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_Greece "Hellenistic Greece") city in [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria_(region) "Syria (region)") of [Antioch on the Orontes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch_on_the_Orontes "Antioch on the Orontes") ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Ἀντιόχεια _Antiocheia_, [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic"): _Antāqiyyah_, now officially [Antakya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antakya "Antakya"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey")). The region of Colombia known as the Coffee Zone has a strong influence from [Arab Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Jews "Arab Jews"), both demographically and culturally, and many towns and cities are named after cities in the Middle East. Moreover, ancient Antioch played a significant role in developing the communities of [early Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Christianity "Early Christianity") and thus was important to the Catholic Spaniard conquistadors.

There are many other cities in the Middle East named [Antiochia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochia_(disambiguation) "Antiochia (disambiguation)"), which were likewise named for the [Antiochid rulers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochus_(disambiguation)#The_Seleucid_Empire "Antiochus (disambiguation)") during the [Seleucid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seleucid_Empire "Seleucid Empire") (312–63 BC).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

### Native people of Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Native people of Antioquia")]

See also: [Columbian exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange "Columbian exchange")

Before Spanish colonization, [Indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_South_America "Indigenous peoples of South America") inhabited the Antioquia region. Some specialists believe they came from [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"), while others say they came from the interior [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River").

Antioquia was primarily populated by the [Kalina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalina_people "Kalina people") or "Mainland Caribs." Some scattered groups of [Muisca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muisca "Muisca") were said to be present in the [Darién](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dari%C3%A9n_Province "Darién Province") region, a coastal region in the far north that is now in [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), but no historical records refer to Muisca in Antioquia.

The Kalina in Antioquia comprised smaller groups called families. The most prominent were the Catía, [Nutabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutabe "Nutabe"), and [Tahamí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taham%C3%AD_people "Tahamí people"), who inhabited central Antioquia. The [Quimbaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimbaya "Quimbaya") occupied southern Antioquia.

The Quimbaya, Kalina, and Muisca were the most prominent groups the [conquistadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador") encountered upon their arrival in Antioquia.

The Spaniards had a turbulent history of encounters with the Carib. Although the tribe was numerous and known for its warring culture, the Spaniards dominated or exterminated them in the process of [conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_(military) "Conquest (military)") and [colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization "Colonization"). Like all [indigenous peoples of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), many died in [virgin soil epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_soil_epidemic "Virgin soil epidemic") of diseases endemic to Eurasia.

Some surviving natives dispersed to evade the Spanish, and some committed suicide to escape [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery"). Many survivors fled to what is now [Chocó department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_department "Chocó department"). Barely 0.5% of Antioquia's population is Indigenous, but most residents have a significant Indigenous genetic component (26% on average).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-7)

### Basque and Jewish influence in Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Basque and Jewish influence in Antioquia")]

[Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")'s [Basque Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_Country_(greater_region) "Basque Country (greater region)") and [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") have influenced Antioquia and its language since the Spanish colonization. This began in 1499 during the [third voyage of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus "Voyages of Christopher Columbus"). The owner and master of the _[Santa María](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_Mar%C3%ADa\_(ship) "Santa María (ship)")_, second in command to Columbus, was [Juan de la Cosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_la_Cosa "Juan de la Cosa"), nicknamed _el Vizcaino_ ("the [Biscayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscay "Biscay")"). Hundreds of [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basques "Basques") settled in the area, sponsored by the Spanish colonization companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-9)

#### Dialect

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dialect")]

Immigrants influenced the Spanish spoken in Antioquia in several ways:

*   Immigrants from [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia") and the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands") brought their preference for _[seseo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seseo "Seseo")_, a uniform pronunciation of "s", "z", and soft "c".
*   However, those from [Extremadura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremadura "Extremadura") favored an [apico-alveolar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolar_fricative#Voiceless_apico-alveolar_sibilant "Voiceless alveolar fricative") sound (part way to "sh").
*   The [digraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") "ll" (double L) is [affricative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affricate "Affricate"), like English "j".
*   Certain words beginning with "r" are [prefixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epenthesis "Epenthesis") by "a" (with the "r" doubled to continue to indicate that it is trilled): 
    *   _arrecostarse_ instead of _recostarse_
    *   _arrecoger_ instead of _recoger_
    *   _arrecordarse_ instead of _recordarse_.

*   Specific words have been adopted, such as _coscorria_ (useless, inept) and _tap_ (tap).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-10)

#### Local character

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Local character")]

It has been asserted since the mid-nineteenth century that Basque and Jewish origins have influenced the character of Antioquia. Specific evidence of cultural contribution is sparse, perhaps partly because Basque is not dominant in Spain.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-11) However, American historian Everett Hagen sampled the Medellín telephone directory in 1957 and found that 15% of the surnames were of Basque origin, but 25% of the employers were. He concluded that Basque influence was important in explaining the increased industrial development of Antioquia in Colombia. The study reinforced notions of the character of social groups, though it has been criticized as stereotypical.

### Spaniards in Antioquia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Spaniards in Antioquia")]

The first Spaniard known to have visited the territory now known as Antioquia was [Rodrigo de Bastidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_de_Bastidas "Rodrigo de Bastidas"), who explored the area around the future site of [Darién](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dari%C3%A9n_Province "Darién Province") in 1500. Ten years later, [Alonso de Ojeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_de_Ojeda "Alonso de Ojeda") founded [San Sebastián de Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n_de_Urab%C3%A1 "San Sebastián de Urabá"), 2 km from the present-day town of [Necoclí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necocl%C3%AD "Necoclí"). It was later destroyed by the natives. The first Spanish military incursion into Antioquia, however, was not made until 1537. An expedition commanded by [Francisco César](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_C%C3%A9sar "Francisco César") traveled through the lands of chief Dabeiba, arriving at the [Cauca River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauca_River "Cauca River"). They were said to have taken important treasures from the indigenous people's tombs. In response, the warriors of chief Nutibara harassed the Spaniards continually, and forced them to return to [Urabá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia").

In 1541, the conquistador [Jorge Robledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Robledo_(conquistador) "Jorge Robledo (conquistador)") departed from the site of the future (1542) Spanish town of Arma, a little below Aguadas in the North of Caldas, to lead an expedition north on the Cauca River.

Farther north, Robledo would found the city of [Santa Fe de Antioquia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_de_Antioquia "Santa Fe de Antioquia"), which in 1813 was declared the capital of the sovereign and independent state of Antioquia, and remained the seat of the governate until 1826, when Medellín was designated the capital.

### 16th to the 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 16th to the 21st centuries")]

Due to its geographical isolation, being located among mountains, Antioquia suffered supply problems. Its topography did not allow for much agriculture, so the city became dependent upon trade, especially of gold and gin for the colonization of new land. Much of this trade was due to reforms passed after a 1785 visit from [Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Antonio_Mon_y_Velarde?action=edit&redlink=1 "Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde (page does not exist)"), an inspector of the Spanish Crown. The Antioquia became colonizers and traders.

The department was hard hit by the [Colombian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_conflict "Colombian conflict"), with 30,000 people missing between 1997 and 2005.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-12)

_[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ and Citi announced in the year 2013 that [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"), the capital of the department of Antioquia, is the winner of the City of the Year competition, a global program developed in partnership with the [Urban Land Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Land_Institute "Urban Land Institute") to recognize the most innovative urban centers. Medellín was ranked above the other finalists, [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv") and [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-14)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Antioquia_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The population of Antioquia is 6,994,792 (2023), of which more than half live in the metropolitan area of [Medellín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medell%C3%ADn "Medellín"). The racial composition is:[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-17)

*   [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people "White people") / [Mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") (88.6%)
*   [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people") or [Afro-Colombian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombians "Colombians") (10.9%)
*   [Indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_in_Colombia "Indigenous peoples in Colombia") or [Amerindian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amerindian "Amerindian") (0.5%)

During the 16th and 18th centuries, Antioquia received many immigrants from Spain, especially [northern Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Spain "Northern Spain").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-19) Most Indigenous peoples died from the introduction of European diseases, and many of those who survived intermarried with early Spanish settlers, who were mostly men; later, Spanish women also began to immigrate. Thousands of Scottish and English who settled in Antioquia fought for the Colombian army during independence.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-20) During the 19th and 20th centuries, immigrants (including Jews)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-21) arrived from Italy, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Portugal, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine and Syria.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-24) Many people from Antioquia are referred to as [Paisas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paisa_Region "Paisa Region"), people of mainly Spanish ancestry, a lot of them Basque.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioquia_Department#cite_note-25) There is a small Afro-Colombian and Zambo-Colombian (people of Indigenous and African descent) population originating in the majority of the [Urabá subregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urab%C3%A1_Antioquia "Urabá Antioquia") and the neighboring departments of [Chocó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choc%C3%B3_Department "Chocó Department"), [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba_Department "Córdoba Department") and [Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre_Department "Sucre Department").

**Santa Cruz** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˌsanta ˈkɾus]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is the largest of the nine constituent departments of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), occupying about one-third (33.74%) of the country's territory. With an area of 370,621 km 2 (143,098 sq mi), it is slightly smaller than [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") or the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") state of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). It is located in the eastern part of the country, sharing borders in the north and east with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and with [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") in the south.

In the 2024 census, it had an estimated population of 3.1 million, making it the most populated department. Its capital city is [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"). The department is one of the wealthiest departments in Bolivia, with huge [reserves of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia"). Besides, it has experienced the highest increase of economic growth during the last 50 years in Bolivia and South America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Government and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Government and administration")]

See also: [List of senators of Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_senators_of_Santa_Cruz "List of senators of Santa Cruz")

According to the current [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"), the highest authority in the department lies with the [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"). The former figure of prefect was appointed by the [President of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") till 2005, when the prefect for the first time was elected by popular vote to serve for a five-year term. In 2010 the first governor was elected according to the implementation of autonomy after a struggle for almost a decade by the people of Santa Cruz.

Santa Cruz also has a Departmental Assembly _(Asamblea Departamental),_ which derives but differs from the previous Departmental Council _(Consejo Departamental)._ It is a state legislature with limited legislation powers, being able to make laws in certain subjects in exclusivity and in some others in concurrence with the state legislative branch.

Satellite images of western [Chiquitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitos_Province "Chiquitos Province") and southern [Ñuflo de Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Ch%C3%A1vez_Province "Ñuflo de Chávez Province") provinces illustrate deforestation from agrarian expansion.

The department covers a vast expanse of territory in eastern Bolivia, much of it [rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"), extending from the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") to the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). The department's economy depends largely on [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), with [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [soybeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soybean "Soybean") and [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") being grown. The amount of land cultivated by modern farming techniques is increasing rapidly in the Santa Cruz area, where weather allows for two crops a year.

In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the [discovery of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia") in the department has led to plans for the development of a regional natural gas industry that is likely to boost the local economy. Bolivia's energy minister said two proposed [liquefied petroleum gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_petroleum_gas "Liquefied petroleum gas") plants may allow the country to boost supplies to Brazil and Argentina by 2010, easing a shortage of the fuel after a lack of investment reduced output. The processing plants would be built in Santa Cruz and each would produce about 200 tons of liquefied petroleum gas a day. The plants would help turn a deficit of gas into a “surplus”.

In July 2004, the people voted in a nationwide [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum "Referendum") to allow for regulated exportation of the gas.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-3)

The department also hosts [El Mutún](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Mut%C3%BAn "El Mutún"), the world's second largest iron ore reserve (after Carajás in Brazil) and largest [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") deposits are also located there. Located in the Germán Busch Province in the Santa Cruz Department of Bolivia, near Puerto Suárez, El Mutún extends across the border into Brazil, where it is called the Serrania de Jacadigo. Also known as the "Serrania Mutún", it has an area of about 75 square kilometers. Its estimated reserves are about 40.205 billion tons of iron ore of 50% iron, mainly in hematite and magnetite form, and in lesser quantities in siderite and manganese minerals. This can be compared with an estimate of the total world reserves of iron ore: 800 billion tons of crude ore containing more than 230 billion tons of iron.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

Santa Cruz Department is the largest of the Bolivian departments and covers a wide and diverse area. In the west lies a series of temperate Sub-Andean ranges and valleys while to the north and south lies two different lowlands areas; the Beni and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") lowlands respectively. To the northeast lies the flat [Llanos Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_Chiquitanos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Llanos Chiquitanos (page does not exist)") areas and beyond these the [Serranías Chiquitanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serran%C3%ADas_Chiquitanas "Serranías Chiquitanas") ranges. In the far east the departments have small parts of the huge [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal") wetland.

The rivers of Santa Cruz are part of any of two basins: the [Amazon Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Basin "Amazon Basin") (north) and the [Plate Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plate Basin (page does not exist)") (south).

The main rivers in the northern basin are [river Iténez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_It%C3%A9nez "River Iténez"), making the border with Brazil, [Río Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_Grande_(Bolivia) "Río Grande (Bolivia)"), [river Piraí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pira%C3%AD_River_(Bolivia) "Piraí River (Bolivia)") and [river Itonomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Itonomas "River Itonomas"). In the southern basin, the main rivers are [river Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Paraguay "River Paraguay") and its tributaries, including [river Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Negro_(Boivia-Paraguay)?action=edit&redlink=1 "River Negro (Boivia-Paraguay) (page does not exist)").

The main lakes are [lake Mandioré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mandior%C3%A9 "Lake Mandioré"), Uberaba, [lake La Gaiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_La_Gaiba "Lake La Gaiba"), [Laguna de Marfil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_de_Marfil "Laguna de Marfil"), Concepción and [lake San Jorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_San_Jorge "Lake San Jorge").

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The first settlers of Santa Cruz were mainly [Spaniards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") that accompanied Ñuflo de Chávez, as well as [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_people "Guarani people"), and some [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people"), [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_people "German people") and [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_people "Italian people") working for the Spanish crown.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-4) Among the first settlers there were also [Sephardic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic "Sephardic")[Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-5) recently converted to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") who were persecuted by the [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquisition "Inquisition") in Spain. Santa Cruz has a multicultural population: 57% are [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") with both Indigenous Amazonian and European ascendants, 30% are Natives ([Chiquitano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano_people "Chiquitano people"), [Chane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chane_people "Chane people"), [Ayoreo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoreo_people "Ayoreo people"), as well as Quechua and Aymara internal migrants from other departments) and 13% are [Whites of European descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Bolivians "White Bolivians"), of whom about a third are the so-called ["Russian" Mennonites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Mennonite "Russian Mennonite") (see [Mennonites in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites_in_Bolivia "Mennonites in Bolivia")) of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") tradition, language and descent.

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Climate")]

At 416 meters above sea level, it is warm and tropical most of the year. Winters are short and last only 2–3 months but can get very cold very suddenly. "Surazos" (southerly winds that blow in from Argentina) can drop the temperature by as much as 30 degrees overnight. This extreme cold lasts only a few days at a time and the beautiful, sub-tropical Santa Cruz is pleasant throughout most of the year. Here the climate varies by geographical zone: temperate to cold in the western sierras and warm to hot and humid as one descends into the extensive plains.

The department of Santa Cruz regularly experiences devastating forest fires, often started by landowners who want to burn forests to create new agricultural land. This practice puts a great strain on the rich biodiversity of the country.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-7)

## Provinces

## Calls for autonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Calls for autonomy")]

During the later stages of the [Chaco war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaco_war "Chaco war") between Paraguay and Bolivia, as the Paraguayan army approached Santa Cruz department, local nationalists backed by a Paraguay-based independence movement sought to create a separate independent state in Santa Cruz department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-9)

[A referendum on autonomy was held in Santa Cruz department in 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_autonomy_referendum,_2008 "Santa Cruz autonomy referendum, 2008"). Eastern departments in Bolivia, including Santa Cruz, have majority of the natural gas reserves. Bolivian president Evo Morales was planning to introduce legislation to tackle the poverty in the country using tax revenues from richer departments like Santa Cruz. Additionally, Morales's attempts to change the constitution were opposed by the opposition governors who run five of Bolivia's nine regions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-10) 85.6 percent voted in favour of autonomy. The Bolivian government considered the referendum illegal.

**Santa Cruz** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˌsanta ˈkɾus]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is the largest of the nine constituent departments of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), occupying about one-third (33.74%) of the country's territory. With an area of 370,621 km 2 (143,098 sq mi), it is slightly smaller than [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") or the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") state of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). It is located in the eastern part of the country, sharing borders in the north and east with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and with [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") in the south.

In the 2024 census, it had an estimated population of 3.1 million, making it the most populated department. Its capital city is [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"). The department is one of the wealthiest departments in Bolivia, with huge [reserves of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia"). Besides, it has experienced the highest increase of economic growth during the last 50 years in Bolivia and South America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Government and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Government and administration")]

See also: [List of senators of Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_senators_of_Santa_Cruz "List of senators of Santa Cruz")

According to the current [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"), the highest authority in the department lies with the [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"). The former figure of prefect was appointed by the [President of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") till 2005, when the prefect for the first time was elected by popular vote to serve for a five-year term. In 2010 the first governor was elected according to the implementation of autonomy after a struggle for almost a decade by the people of Santa Cruz.

Santa Cruz also has a Departmental Assembly _(Asamblea Departamental),_ which derives but differs from the previous Departmental Council _(Consejo Departamental)._ It is a state legislature with limited legislation powers, being able to make laws in certain subjects in exclusivity and in some others in concurrence with the state legislative branch.

Satellite images of western [Chiquitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitos_Province "Chiquitos Province") and southern [Ñuflo de Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Ch%C3%A1vez_Province "Ñuflo de Chávez Province") provinces illustrate deforestation from agrarian expansion.

The department covers a vast expanse of territory in eastern Bolivia, much of it [rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"), extending from the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") to the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). The department's economy depends largely on [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), with [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [soybeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soybean "Soybean") and [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") being grown. The amount of land cultivated by modern farming techniques is increasing rapidly in the Santa Cruz area, where weather allows for two crops a year.

In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the [discovery of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia") in the department has led to plans for the development of a regional natural gas industry that is likely to boost the local economy. Bolivia's energy minister said two proposed [liquefied petroleum gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_petroleum_gas "Liquefied petroleum gas") plants may allow the country to boost supplies to Brazil and Argentina by 2010, easing a shortage of the fuel after a lack of investment reduced output. The processing plants would be built in Santa Cruz and each would produce about 200 tons of liquefied petroleum gas a day. The plants would help turn a deficit of gas into a “surplus”.

In July 2004, the people voted in a nationwide [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum "Referendum") to allow for regulated exportation of the gas.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-3)

The department also hosts [El Mutún](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Mut%C3%BAn "El Mutún"), the world's second largest iron ore reserve (after Carajás in Brazil) and largest [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") deposits are also located there. Located in the Germán Busch Province in the Santa Cruz Department of Bolivia, near Puerto Suárez, El Mutún extends across the border into Brazil, where it is called the Serrania de Jacadigo. Also known as the "Serrania Mutún", it has an area of about 75 square kilometers. Its estimated reserves are about 40.205 billion tons of iron ore of 50% iron, mainly in hematite and magnetite form, and in lesser quantities in siderite and manganese minerals. This can be compared with an estimate of the total world reserves of iron ore: 800 billion tons of crude ore containing more than 230 billion tons of iron.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

Santa Cruz Department is the largest of the Bolivian departments and covers a wide and diverse area. In the west lies a series of temperate Sub-Andean ranges and valleys while to the north and south lies two different lowlands areas; the Beni and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") lowlands respectively. To the northeast lies the flat [Llanos Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_Chiquitanos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Llanos Chiquitanos (page does not exist)") areas and beyond these the [Serranías Chiquitanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serran%C3%ADas_Chiquitanas "Serranías Chiquitanas") ranges. In the far east the departments have small parts of the huge [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal") wetland.

The rivers of Santa Cruz are part of any of two basins: the [Amazon Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Basin "Amazon Basin") (north) and the [Plate Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plate Basin (page does not exist)") (south).

The main rivers in the northern basin are [river Iténez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_It%C3%A9nez "River Iténez"), making the border with Brazil, [Río Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_Grande_(Bolivia) "Río Grande (Bolivia)"), [river Piraí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pira%C3%AD_River_(Bolivia) "Piraí River (Bolivia)") and [river Itonomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Itonomas "River Itonomas"). In the southern basin, the main rivers are [river Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Paraguay "River Paraguay") and its tributaries, including [river Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Negro_(Boivia-Paraguay)?action=edit&redlink=1 "River Negro (Boivia-Paraguay) (page does not exist)").

The main lakes are [lake Mandioré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mandior%C3%A9 "Lake Mandioré"), Uberaba, [lake La Gaiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_La_Gaiba "Lake La Gaiba"), [Laguna de Marfil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_de_Marfil "Laguna de Marfil"), Concepción and [lake San Jorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_San_Jorge "Lake San Jorge").

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The first settlers of Santa Cruz were mainly [Spaniards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") that accompanied Ñuflo de Chávez, as well as [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_people "Guarani people"), and some [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people"), [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_people "German people") and [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_people "Italian people") working for the Spanish crown.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-4) Among the first settlers there were also [Sephardic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic "Sephardic")[Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-5) recently converted to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") who were persecuted by the [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquisition "Inquisition") in Spain. Santa Cruz has a multicultural population: 57% are [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") with both Indigenous Amazonian and European ascendants, 30% are Natives ([Chiquitano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano_people "Chiquitano people"), [Chane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chane_people "Chane people"), [Ayoreo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoreo_people "Ayoreo people"), as well as Quechua and Aymara internal migrants from other departments) and 13% are [Whites of European descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Bolivians "White Bolivians"), of whom about a third are the so-called ["Russian" Mennonites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Mennonite "Russian Mennonite") (see [Mennonites in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites_in_Bolivia "Mennonites in Bolivia")) of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") tradition, language and descent.

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Climate")]

At 416 meters above sea level, it is warm and tropical most of the year. Winters are short and last only 2–3 months but can get very cold very suddenly. "Surazos" (southerly winds that blow in from Argentina) can drop the temperature by as much as 30 degrees overnight. This extreme cold lasts only a few days at a time and the beautiful, sub-tropical Santa Cruz is pleasant throughout most of the year. Here the climate varies by geographical zone: temperate to cold in the western sierras and warm to hot and humid as one descends into the extensive plains.

The department of Santa Cruz regularly experiences devastating forest fires, often started by landowners who want to burn forests to create new agricultural land. This practice puts a great strain on the rich biodiversity of the country.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-7)

## Calls for autonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Calls for autonomy")]

During the later stages of the [Chaco war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaco_war "Chaco war") between Paraguay and Bolivia, as the Paraguayan army approached Santa Cruz department, local nationalists backed by a Paraguay-based independence movement sought to create a separate independent state in Santa Cruz department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-9)

[A referendum on autonomy was held in Santa Cruz department in 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_autonomy_referendum,_2008 "Santa Cruz autonomy referendum, 2008"). Eastern departments in Bolivia, including Santa Cruz, have majority of the natural gas reserves. Bolivian president Evo Morales was planning to introduce legislation to tackle the poverty in the country using tax revenues from richer departments like Santa Cruz. Additionally, Morales's attempts to change the constitution were opposed by the opposition governors who run five of Bolivia's nine regions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-10) 85.6 percent voted in favour of autonomy. The Bolivian government considered the referendum illegal.

**Chuquisaca** (Spanish pronunciation:[[tʃukiˈsaka]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_language "Guarani language"): _Chuquisaca_; [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Chuqichaka_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Chuqisaka_) is a department of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") located in the center south. It borders on the departments of Cochabamba, [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department"), [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department "Potosí Department"), and [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)"). The departmental [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(political) "Capital (political)") is [Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre,_Bolivia "Sucre, Bolivia"), which is also the constitutional capital of Bolivia.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

The department is traversed by the main [cordillera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range and lesser cordilleras. Parts of it lay within the basin of the [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River"), and other parts within the basin of the [Río de La Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_de_La_Plata "Río de La Plata"). The surface area of the department is 51,524 square kilometers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3) The topography of central Chuquisaca consists of a series of ridges rising up to 1500 m that run north and south with flat valleys between the ridges. To the west of these ridges abruptly rise the Andes Mountains to 3000 m forming a [prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") landmass that is cut into by large river valleys that drain into the Amazon or Rio de la Plata river basins. To the east of the central ridges lies a stretch of territory containing low elevation flat [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") topography.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4) 90% of the land in the department of Chuquisaca has an inclination of 70% or more.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3)

## Ecological and vegetation zones

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ecological and vegetation zones")]

[![Image 11: Map of Chuquisaca showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Chuquisaca, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Ecological and vegetation zones in the department of Chuquisaca vary widely according to a diversity of abiotic factors including [soil formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_formation "Soil formation") and textures, rainfall patterns, and mineral and salinity content of water. Elevation plays an important role in the dispersion of vegetation species and wider ecosystems as they respond to microclimates. As the Andes Mountains became uplifted, plants adapted to dryer and higher microclimates resulting in a high level of speciation especially in the dry forest river valleys of the Bolivian-Tucuman formation.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6) colder and drier air from more austral parts of South America have resulted in migration of plant communities with a floristic connection to those in Argentina, Paraguay and Southern Brazil as opposed to more tropical plant communities that result from warm and moist northern climates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6) Navarro and Ferreira have developed a database of plant species in Bolivia[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7) and identified 39 separate vegetation zones in Bolivia within twelve general physiographic-biogeographical units of which four fall in the boundaries of Chuquisaca Department including: [Cordillera Oriental Central y Meridional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Oriental_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Oriental (Bolivia)"), [Prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") or High Interandean Valleys, Bolivian-Tucuman Formation, and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco"). Using Navarro and Ferreira's categories and descriptions based on vegetation zones, the geographical and ecological characteristics of the Chuquisaca Department can be described as follows.

[Cordillera Oriental Central y Meridional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Oriental_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Oriental (Bolivia)"). From an elevation of 3200m in Chuquisaca to nearly 6000 meters in Potosi, this zone is characterized by the puna, altoandean, and subnival and nival ecological zones with a pluviestacional subhumid bioclimate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

[Prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") or High Interandean Valley. From 2300m to 3200m, this zone is characterized by a mesotropical [dry xeric bioclimatic zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_montane_dry_forests "Bolivian montane dry forests"). Seasonally torrential waters and salinity levels affect regional vegetation patterns in this zone.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

Bolivian-Tucuman Formation. With a wide elevation range between 600m to 3900m this zone contains pluviestacional subhumid and locally humid bioclimatic zones. The high elevation Rio Grande and Pilcomayo river valleys transect this unit and are characterized by dry xeric vegetation zones with endemic and varied speciation especially in the Rio Grande river valley and vegetation influence from the Chaco in the Pilcomayo river valley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7) Wet forest ecosystems like those found in more northern [Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Andean_Yungas "Southern Andean Yungas") valleys are found on high ridges where clouds form.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto,_Bolivia.jpg)

Xeric River Valley near Presto, Bolivia

[Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco"): from 400 to 900 m this unit is characterized by a xeric bioclimate. Sandy soils in this unit were formed from alluvial processes from the Parapeti and Grande rivers. Soil drainage affects vegetation dispersion within this unit.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

## Human Ecological Impacts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Human Ecological Impacts")]

With a human population of 631,000 people[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-8) humans are a part of the ecology of Chuquisaca. The grazing of cattle and introduction of invasive feral citrus trees has affected the native plant populations in the department.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4) Native forests and ecosystems have contracted as land has been converted to pasture and erosion is widespread as a result of human agricultural activities on steep slopes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-9)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010. The majority party in the twenty-one member assembly after the first election was held by the Movement towards Socialism (MAS-IPSP) with 15 seats. Four seats were held by [We Are All Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Are_All_Chuquisaca "We Are All Chuquisaca"). Two seats were selected by the Guaraní people through _[usos y costumbres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usos\_y\_costumbres "Usos y costumbres")_.

The [last elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") to the Departmental Legislative Assembly took place on 1 March 2021 for seats reserved for the [Guaraní people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaran%C3%AD_people "Guaraní people") and 7 March for the regular seats.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-11) The current executive committee, elected on 28 April 2022, consists of Santos Ricardo Carnicel Serrano as president, Evert Cruz Quiroga as first vice-president, Janeth Rocio Blanco Martínez as second vice-president, Juan Cuellar as first secretary and Anastacio Flores Pinto as second secretary.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-12)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: History")]

The native inhabitants were the Charcas, who were dispersed along riverbanks and lowlands. Their leaders, _jampiris_, sorcerers, and priests resided in the capital, [Choque-Chaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choque-Chaca?action=edit&redlink=1 "Choque-Chaca (page does not exist)"), which according to 17th century chronicles had a population of several thousand.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The eastern lowlands of the department, where the autonomous [Ava Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ava_Guarani_people "Ava Guarani people") resided, started a gradual but forcefull incorporation to the Bolivian state in the 1850s.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023346-13) The non-indigenous settlement in eastern Chuquisaca was motivated by an expansion of cattle ranching leading contributing to the conflict between settlers and the maize-farming Ava Guaraní to assume aspects of a [farmer–herder conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmer%E2%80%93herder_conflict "Farmer–herder conflict").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023349-14) A major Ava Guaraní uprising took place in 1874[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023353-15) and a final military defeat came in 1892.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023359-16)[Aniceto Arce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniceto_Arce "Aniceto Arce") and other wealthy Bolivians gained control of lands of the defeated Ava Guaraní in the late 19th century establsining large cattle farming operations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023360-17) Much of the cattle raised in eastern Chuquisaca was exported to [Salta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salta "Salta") in Argentina and then across the Andes to the [saltpeter works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_saltpeter_works_in_Tarapac%C3%A1_and_Antofagasta "List of saltpeter works in Tarapacá and Antofagasta") in Chile's [Atacama Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert "Atacama Desert").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023359-16) Given the massivity of the cattle estates established Franciscan friar Angélico Martarelli argued around 1890 that the Chiriguano lands had been colonized by cattle rather than by settlers.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023360-17)

### Sucre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sucre")]

[Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre "Sucre") (elev. 2750 m) is called the city of the four names, each name corresponding to a different period of its history. It was founded by the Spaniard [Pedro de Anzures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Anzures?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pedro de Anzures (page does not exist)") in 1538. It thrived due to its regional proximity to the famous silver mines of Potosi, and as _Charcas_ served as capital of the Real Audiencia de Charcas, encompassing all of current Bolivia's territory and more. Reverting to its native name of Chuquisaca, it was the Upper Peru's chief administrative center and largest city. It was there that the first public call for independence from Spain took place, on May 25, 1809, and where the Act of Independence from Spanish rule was signed on August 6, 1825. It was immediately designated the capital of independent Bolivia, under the auspices of Simon Bolivar and Antonio Jose de Sucre. Years later, the city of Chuquisaca was renamed Sucre in honor of the Venezuelan-born hero of South America's independence, who had served as the first effective administrator of the country (and second president).

When the center of political and economic power shifted north, to the tin-producing regions of Oruro and La Paz, Sucre's importance waned, leading to the displacement of the legislative and executive powers to La Paz. However, in honor of Sucre's historical preponderance, the judicial branch (Supreme Court) continues to operate there, and the city's official status as capital of the country was never revoked.

**Chuquisaca** (Spanish pronunciation:[[tʃukiˈsaka]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_language "Guarani language"): _Chuquisaca_; [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Chuqichaka_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Chuqisaka_) is a department of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") located in the center south. It borders on the departments of Cochabamba, [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department"), [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department "Potosí Department"), and [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)"). The departmental [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(political) "Capital (political)") is [Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre,_Bolivia "Sucre, Bolivia"), which is also the constitutional capital of Bolivia.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

The department is traversed by the main [cordillera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range and lesser cordilleras. Parts of it lay within the basin of the [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River"), and other parts within the basin of the [Río de La Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_de_La_Plata "Río de La Plata"). The surface area of the department is 51,524 square kilometers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3) The topography of central Chuquisaca consists of a series of ridges rising up to 1500 m that run north and south with flat valleys between the ridges. To the west of these ridges abruptly rise the Andes Mountains to 3000 m forming a [prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") landmass that is cut into by large river valleys that drain into the Amazon or Rio de la Plata river basins. To the east of the central ridges lies a stretch of territory containing low elevation flat [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") topography.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4) 90% of the land in the department of Chuquisaca has an inclination of 70% or more.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3)

## Ecological and vegetation zones

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ecological and vegetation zones")]

[![Image 11: Map of Chuquisaca showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Chuquisaca,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Chuquisaca, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Ecological and vegetation zones in the department of Chuquisaca vary widely according to a diversity of abiotic factors including [soil formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_formation "Soil formation") and textures, rainfall patterns, and mineral and salinity content of water. Elevation plays an important role in the dispersion of vegetation species and wider ecosystems as they respond to microclimates. As the Andes Mountains became uplifted, plants adapted to dryer and higher microclimates resulting in a high level of speciation especially in the dry forest river valleys of the Bolivian-Tucuman formation.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6) colder and drier air from more austral parts of South America have resulted in migration of plant communities with a floristic connection to those in Argentina, Paraguay and Southern Brazil as opposed to more tropical plant communities that result from warm and moist northern climates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6) Navarro and Ferreira have developed a database of plant species in Bolivia[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7) and identified 39 separate vegetation zones in Bolivia within twelve general physiographic-biogeographical units of which four fall in the boundaries of Chuquisaca Department including: [Cordillera Oriental Central y Meridional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Oriental_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Oriental (Bolivia)"), [Prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") or High Interandean Valleys, Bolivian-Tucuman Formation, and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco"). Using Navarro and Ferreira's categories and descriptions based on vegetation zones, the geographical and ecological characteristics of the Chuquisaca Department can be described as follows.

[Cordillera Oriental Central y Meridional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Oriental_(Bolivia) "Cordillera Oriental (Bolivia)"). From an elevation of 3200m in Chuquisaca to nearly 6000 meters in Potosi, this zone is characterized by the puna, altoandean, and subnival and nival ecological zones with a pluviestacional subhumid bioclimate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

[Prepuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prepuna (page does not exist)") or High Interandean Valley. From 2300m to 3200m, this zone is characterized by a mesotropical [dry xeric bioclimatic zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_montane_dry_forests "Bolivian montane dry forests"). Seasonally torrential waters and salinity levels affect regional vegetation patterns in this zone.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

Bolivian-Tucuman Formation. With a wide elevation range between 600m to 3900m this zone contains pluviestacional subhumid and locally humid bioclimatic zones. The high elevation Rio Grande and Pilcomayo river valleys transect this unit and are characterized by dry xeric vegetation zones with endemic and varied speciation especially in the Rio Grande river valley and vegetation influence from the Chaco in the Pilcomayo river valley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Lopez_2003-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7) Wet forest ecosystems like those found in more northern [Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Andean_Yungas "Southern Andean Yungas") valleys are found on high ridges where clouds form.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xeric_River_Valley_near_Presto,_Bolivia.jpg)

[Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco"): from 400 to 900 m this unit is characterized by a xeric bioclimate. Sandy soils in this unit were formed from alluvial processes from the Parapeti and Grande rivers. Soil drainage affects vegetation dispersion within this unit.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Navarro_2004-7)

## Human Ecological Impacts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Human Ecological Impacts")]

With a human population of 631,000 people[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-8) humans are a part of the ecology of Chuquisaca. The grazing of cattle and introduction of invasive feral citrus trees has affected the native plant populations in the department.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-Schulenberg_1997-4) Native forests and ecosystems have contracted as land has been converted to pasture and erosion is widespread as a result of human agricultural activities on steep slopes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-sitap.produccion.gob.bo-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-9)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010. The majority party in the twenty-one member assembly after the first election was held by the Movement towards Socialism (MAS-IPSP) with 15 seats. Four seats were held by [We Are All Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Are_All_Chuquisaca "We Are All Chuquisaca"). Two seats were selected by the Guaraní people through _[usos y costumbres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usos\_y\_costumbres "Usos y costumbres")_.

The [last elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") to the Departmental Legislative Assembly took place on 1 March 2021 for seats reserved for the [Guaraní people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaran%C3%AD_people "Guaraní people") and 7 March for the regular seats.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-11) The current executive committee, elected on 28 April 2022, consists of Santos Ricardo Carnicel Serrano as president, Evert Cruz Quiroga as first vice-president, Janeth Rocio Blanco Martínez as second vice-president, Juan Cuellar as first secretary and Anastacio Flores Pinto as second secretary.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-12)

Further information: [List of senators of Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_senators_of_Chuquisaca "List of senators of Chuquisaca")

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: History")]

The native inhabitants were the Charcas, who were dispersed along riverbanks and lowlands. Their leaders, _jampiris_, sorcerers, and priests resided in the capital, [Choque-Chaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choque-Chaca?action=edit&redlink=1 "Choque-Chaca (page does not exist)"), which according to 17th century chronicles had a population of several thousand.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The eastern lowlands of the department, where the autonomous [Ava Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ava_Guarani_people "Ava Guarani people") resided, started a gradual but forcefull incorporation to the Bolivian state in the 1850s.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023346-13) The non-indigenous settlement in eastern Chuquisaca was motivated by an expansion of cattle ranching leading contributing to the conflict between settlers and the maize-farming Ava Guaraní to assume aspects of a [farmer–herder conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmer%E2%80%93herder_conflict "Farmer–herder conflict").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023349-14) A major Ava Guaraní uprising took place in 1874[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023353-15) and a final military defeat came in 1892.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023359-16)[Aniceto Arce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniceto_Arce "Aniceto Arce") and other wealthy Bolivians gained control of lands of the defeated Ava Guaraní in the late 19th century establsining large cattle farming operations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023360-17) Much of the cattle raised in eastern Chuquisaca was exported to [Salta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salta "Salta") in Argentina and then across the Andes to the [saltpeter works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_saltpeter_works_in_Tarapac%C3%A1_and_Antofagasta "List of saltpeter works in Tarapacá and Antofagasta") in Chile's [Atacama Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert "Atacama Desert").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023359-16) Given the massivity of the cattle estates established Franciscan friar Angélico Martarelli argued around 1890 that the Chiriguano lands had been colonized by cattle rather than by settlers.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department#cite_note-FOOTNOTETapia_MatamalaPrieto_Serrano2023360-17)

### Sucre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chuquisaca_Department&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sucre")]

[Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre "Sucre") (elev. 2750 m) is called the city of the four names, each name corresponding to a different period of its history. It was founded by the Spaniard [Pedro de Anzures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Anzures?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pedro de Anzures (page does not exist)") in 1538. It thrived due to its regional proximity to the famous silver mines of Potosi, and as _Charcas_ served as capital of the Real Audiencia de Charcas, encompassing all of current Bolivia's territory and more. Reverting to its native name of Chuquisaca, it was the Upper Peru's chief administrative center and largest city. It was there that the first public call for independence from Spain took place, on May 25, 1809, and where the Act of Independence from Spanish rule was signed on August 6, 1825. It was immediately designated the capital of independent Bolivia, under the auspices of Simon Bolivar and Antonio Jose de Sucre. Years later, the city of Chuquisaca was renamed Sucre in honor of the Venezuelan-born hero of South America's independence, who had served as the first effective administrator of the country (and second president).

When the center of political and economic power shifted north, to the tin-producing regions of Oruro and La Paz, Sucre's importance waned, leading to the displacement of the legislative and executive powers to La Paz. However, in honor of Sucre's historical preponderance, the judicial branch (Supreme Court) continues to operate there, and the city's official status as capital of the country was never revoked.
