**Potosí** (Spanish pronunciation:[[potoˈsi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Quechua "Southern Quechua"): _P'utuqsi_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Putusi_) is a department in southwestern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its area is 118,218 km 2 (45,644 sq mi) and its population is 856,419 (2024 census). The capital is the city of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). It is a mostly barren, mountainous region with one large [plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau") to the west, where the largest [salt flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") in the world, [Salar de Uyuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni "Salar de Uyuni"), is located.

[Cerro Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico") was the richest province in the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), providing a great percentage of the [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") that was [shipped to Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleet "Spanish treasure fleet").

Potosi is also the location of the [San Cristóbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Crist%C3%B3bal_mine_(Bolivia) "San Cristóbal mine (Bolivia)") silver, zinc and lead mines, developed by the US company Apex Silver Mines Limited of Colorado and sold in November 2008 to the Japanese [Sumitomo Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation").

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James's_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada,_Bolivia.jpg)

[Laguna Colorada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Colorada "Laguna Colorada") with [flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamingo "Flamingo") in the [Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Avaroa_Andean_Fauna_National_Reserve "Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In March 2023, social organisations in four regions of Potosí, with the support of regional [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAS-IPSP "MAS-IPSP") lawmakers, called for a strike spanning over 72 hours, to force the government to raise infrastructure investments in the department and to receive an increased amount of the profits generated through lithium mining in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-a21-3) Shortly after the strike an agreement with the central government was reached, stipulating the construction of motorways and a cement plant and further discussions about mining conditions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-a21-3)

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Bolivian_regional_elections "2010 Bolivian regional elections") were held 4 April 2010.

The current executive committee consists of Jacinto Sunagua Dorado as president, Raimunda Cordero Caba as vice-president and Alberto Quispe Mamani as secretary and Blanca Celia Burgos Quispe and Leon Jancko Condori as first and second committee member, respectively.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-5)

**Potosí** (Spanish pronunciation:[[potoˈsi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Quechua "Southern Quechua"): _P'utuqsi_; [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Putusi_) is a department in southwestern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its area is 118,218 km 2 (45,644 sq mi) and its population is 856,419 (2024 census). The capital is the city of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). It is a mostly barren, mountainous region with one large [plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau") to the west, where the largest [salt flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_pan_(geology) "Salt pan (geology)") in the world, [Salar de Uyuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni "Salar de Uyuni"), is located.

[Cerro Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico") was the richest province in the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), providing a great percentage of the [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") that was [shipped to Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleet "Spanish treasure fleet").

Potosi is also the location of the [San Cristóbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Crist%C3%B3bal_mine_(Bolivia) "San Cristóbal mine (Bolivia)") silver, zinc and lead mines, developed by the US company Apex Silver Mines Limited of Colorado and sold in November 2008 to the Japanese [Sumitomo Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation").

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-James%27s_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James's_Flamingoes_in_Laguna_Colorada,_Bolivia.jpg)

[Laguna Colorada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Colorada "Laguna Colorada") with [flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamingo "Flamingo") in the [Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Avaroa_Andean_Fauna_National_Reserve "Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In March 2023, social organisations in four regions of Potosí, with the support of regional [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAS-IPSP "MAS-IPSP") lawmakers, called for a strike spanning over 72 hours, to force the government to raise infrastructure investments in the department and to receive an increased amount of the profits generated through lithium mining in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-a21-3) Shortly after the strike an agreement with the central government was reached, stipulating the construction of motorways and a cement plant and further discussions about mining conditions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-a21-3)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, each Bolivian department has an elected Departmental Legislative Assembly. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Bolivian_regional_elections "2010 Bolivian regional elections") were held 4 April 2010.

The current executive committee consists of Jacinto Sunagua Dorado as president, Raimunda Cordero Caba as vice-president and Alberto Quispe Mamani as secretary and Blanca Celia Burgos Quispe and Leon Jancko Condori as first and second committee member, respectively.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department#cite_note-5)

**Pando** is a [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(country_subdivision) "Department (country subdivision)") in Northern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), with an area of 63,827 square kilometres (24,644 sq mi), in the [Amazon rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_rainforest "Amazon rainforest"), adjoining the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and [Perú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"). Pando has a population of 130,761 (2024 census).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-3) Its capital is the city of [Cobija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobija "Cobija").

The department, named after former president [José Manuel Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Manuel_Pando "José Manuel Pando") (1899–1905), is divided into five provinces. Although Pando is rich in natural resources, the poverty level of its inhabitants is high, due largely to the lack of roads effectively linking the province to the rest of the country. In addition, residents suffer from debilitating effects of tropical diseases, typical of life in the Amazonian rain forest. The main economic activities are agriculture, timber, and cattle.

At an altitude of 280 metres above sea level in the northwestern jungle region, Pando is located in the rainiest part of Bolivia. Pando has a hot climate, with temperatures commonly above 26 degrees Celsius (80 Fahrenheit). It is the least populous department in Bolivia, the most tropical (lying closest to the Equator in the Amazonian Basin), and the most isolated, due to an absence of effective roads. It was organized at the beginning of the 20th century from what was left of the Acre Territory, lost to Brazil as a result of the so-called [Acre War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acre_War "Acre War") (1903). Its capital city of [Cobija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobija "Cobija") (the smallest of all the Bolivian departmental capitals) was named after the much-lamented Bolivian port of the same name on the Pacific Ocean, part of an area lost to [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") following the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific").

[![Image 10: Map of Pando showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Pando, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Although remote, Pando is densely forested and close to navigable waterways leading to the [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River") and from there on to the Atlantic Ocean. The department had a [rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber "Rubber")[boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_boom "Economic boom") in the late 19th century and early 20th century, along with the northern part of the nearby Beni department. The local industry collapsed under competition with rubber cultivated in Southeast Asia, as well as the discovery and manufacture of [synthetic rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_rubber "Synthetic rubber").

Culturally, the Pandinos are considered part of the so-called [Camba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camba "Camba") culture of the Bolivian lowlands, similar to the people of the country's other two tropical departments, Beni and Santa Cruz. Many of Pando's original settlers moved from nearby Beni.

## Autonomy movement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pando_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Autonomy movement")]

Far from the centers of power in Bolivian society, Pando has recently linked its fate with that of Santa Cruz and Beni, which (along with Tarija and Chuquisaca) are demanding increased autonomy for the departments, with a lessening in central government power. Prefect [Leopoldo Fernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Fern%C3%A1ndez "Leopoldo Fernández") strongly backed autonomy for the department, in alliance with other governors of the eastern _media luna_ (half-moon, so known for their combined geographic shape). Nationwide referendums on autonomy held on July 2, 2006, were approved in all four departments. A second referendum to approve a statute of autonomy was held by each department in mid-2008, despite being declared illegal by the National Electoral Court in March. Left-wing and pro-Morales social movements boycotted the votes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-4)

Pando's referendum, held on June 1, 2008, won 82% approval among those who voted. But 46.5% of the registered electorate did not vote, the highest abstention rate in the four departments holding such referendums.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-5) Considerable social unrest took place in 2008, culminating with the arrest in September 2008 of Prefect Leopoldo Fernández, stemming from the [massacre at El Porvenir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porvenir_Massacre "Porvenir Massacre") of anti-autonomy backers of President [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-6)

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pando_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

The chief executive office of Bolivia departments (since May 2010) is the governor; until then, the office was called the prefect, and until 2006 the prefect was appointed by the [President of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). ### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pando_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, a Departmental Legislative Assembly was instituted for each Bolivian department. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") hereunto were held on 4 April 2010. The legislature has 21 members. Its current composition, per the [last regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections"), is 13 seats for the [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism%E2%80%93Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples?action=edit&redlink=1 "Movement for Socialism–Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples (page does not exist)"), 3 for indigenous representatives, 2 for the Democratic Integration Community and one each for [MTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_System_Movement?action=edit&redlink=1 "Third System Movement (page does not exist)"), _Movimiento Democrático Autonomista_ and We Are All Pando.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-pda-10)

The current executive committee was determined per vote on 2 May 2022, selecting Olga Feliciano Ampuero as president, Almir Flores Muzumbite as vice-president, Josué Olmos Quetehuari as secretary and Keila Tirina Peralta and Georgina Ribero Chao as first and second committee member, respectively.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-pda-10)

**Pando** is a [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(country_subdivision) "Department (country subdivision)") in Northern [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), with an area of 63,827 square kilometres (24,644 sq mi), in the [Amazon rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_rainforest "Amazon rainforest"), adjoining the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and [Perú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"). Pando has a population of 130,761 (2024 census).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-3) Its capital is the city of [Cobija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobija "Cobija").

The department, named after former president [José Manuel Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Manuel_Pando "José Manuel Pando") (1899–1905), is divided into five provinces. Although Pando is rich in natural resources, the poverty level of its inhabitants is high, due largely to the lack of roads effectively linking the province to the rest of the country. In addition, residents suffer from debilitating effects of tropical diseases, typical of life in the Amazonian rain forest. The main economic activities are agriculture, timber, and cattle.

At an altitude of 280 metres above sea level in the northwestern jungle region, Pando is located in the rainiest part of Bolivia. Pando has a hot climate, with temperatures commonly above 26 degrees Celsius (80 Fahrenheit). It is the least populous department in Bolivia, the most tropical (lying closest to the Equator in the Amazonian Basin), and the most isolated, due to an absence of effective roads. It was organized at the beginning of the 20th century from what was left of the Acre Territory, lost to Brazil as a result of the so-called [Acre War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acre_War "Acre War") (1903). Its capital city of [Cobija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobija "Cobija") (the smallest of all the Bolivian departmental capitals) was named after the much-lamented Bolivian port of the same name on the Pacific Ocean, part of an area lost to [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") following the [War of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Pacific "War of the Pacific").

[![Image 10: Map of Pando showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Pando,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Pando, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Although remote, Pando is densely forested and close to navigable waterways leading to the [Amazon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River") and from there on to the Atlantic Ocean. The department had a [rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber "Rubber")[boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_boom "Economic boom") in the late 19th century and early 20th century, along with the northern part of the nearby Beni department. The local industry collapsed under competition with rubber cultivated in Southeast Asia, as well as the discovery and manufacture of [synthetic rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_rubber "Synthetic rubber").

Culturally, the Pandinos are considered part of the so-called [Camba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camba "Camba") culture of the Bolivian lowlands, similar to the people of the country's other two tropical departments, Beni and Santa Cruz. Many of Pando's original settlers moved from nearby Beni.

## Autonomy movement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pando_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Autonomy movement")]

Far from the centers of power in Bolivian society, Pando has recently linked its fate with that of Santa Cruz and Beni, which (along with Tarija and Chuquisaca) are demanding increased autonomy for the departments, with a lessening in central government power. Prefect [Leopoldo Fernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldo_Fern%C3%A1ndez "Leopoldo Fernández") strongly backed autonomy for the department, in alliance with other governors of the eastern _media luna_ (half-moon, so known for their combined geographic shape). Nationwide referendums on autonomy held on July 2, 2006, were approved in all four departments. A second referendum to approve a statute of autonomy was held by each department in mid-2008, despite being declared illegal by the National Electoral Court in March. Left-wing and pro-Morales social movements boycotted the votes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-4)

Pando's referendum, held on June 1, 2008, won 82% approval among those who voted. But 46.5% of the registered electorate did not vote, the highest abstention rate in the four departments holding such referendums.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-5) Considerable social unrest took place in 2008, culminating with the arrest in September 2008 of Prefect Leopoldo Fernández, stemming from the [massacre at El Porvenir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porvenir_Massacre "Porvenir Massacre") of anti-autonomy backers of President [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-6)

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pando_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the 2009 Constitution, a Departmental Legislative Assembly was instituted for each Bolivian department. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") hereunto were held on 4 April 2010. The legislature has 21 members. Its current composition, per the [last regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections"), is 13 seats for the [MAS-IPSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism%E2%80%93Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples?action=edit&redlink=1 "Movement for Socialism–Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples (page does not exist)"), 3 for indigenous representatives, 2 for the Democratic Integration Community and one each for [MTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_System_Movement?action=edit&redlink=1 "Third System Movement (page does not exist)"), _Movimiento Democrático Autonomista_ and We Are All Pando.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-pda-10)

The current executive committee was determined per vote on 2 May 2022, selecting Olga Feliciano Ampuero as president, Almir Flores Muzumbite as vice-president, Josué Olmos Quetehuari as secretary and Keila Tirina Peralta and Georgina Ribero Chao as first and second committee member, respectively.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department#cite_note-pda-10)

_**Coffea arabica**_ ([/ə ˈ r æ b ɪ k ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")), also known as the **Arabica coffee**, is a species of [flowering plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant "Flowering plant") in the [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and madder family [Rubiaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubiaceae "Rubiaceae"). It is believed to be the first species of coffee to have been cultivated and is the dominant cultivar, representing about 60% of global production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-CoffeeProduction-2) Coffee produced from the less acidic, more bitter, and more highly [caffeinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeinated "Caffeinated") robusta bean (_[C. canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_) makes up most of the remaining coffee production. The natural populations of _Coffea arabica_ are restricted to the forests of [South Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Ethiopia "South Ethiopia"), [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"), and [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-5)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

Wild plants grow between 9 and 12 m (30 and 39 ft) tall, and have an open branching system; the [leaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") are opposite, simple elliptic-ovate to oblong, 6–12 cm (2.5–4.5 in) long and 4–8 cm (1.5–3 in) broad, glossy dark green, with prominent veins and wavy margins.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-6)

The [flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower "Flower") are white, 10–15 mm in diameter, and grow in axillary clusters of 2 to 9. The fruit is a [drupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drupe "Drupe") (commonly called a "cherry") 10–15 mm in diameter, maturing bright red to purple and typically containing two [seeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seed "Seed") each which become [coffee beans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_bean "Coffee bean").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-8)

## Taxonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Taxonomy")]

The botanical name _Coffea arabica_ was formally published by [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") in his _[Species plantarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species\_plantarum "Species plantarum")_ in 1753.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-9) The species had been described and depicted before, as Linnaeus was able to refer to [Antoine de Jussieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_de_Jussieu "Antoine de Jussieu"), who named it _Jasminum arabicum_, published in 1715, after studying a specimen sent to him from the [Botanic Garden of Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hortus_Botanicus_(Amsterdam) "Hortus Botanicus (Amsterdam)"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-11)[Gaspard Bauhin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspard_Bauhin "Gaspard Bauhin")'s _Pinax_ of 1623 under 'Evonymus IV'[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-12) and [Prospero Alpini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospero_Alpini "Prospero Alpini")'s _De plantis Aegypti liber_, published in 1592.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-13)

_Coffea arabica_ is one of the [polyploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyploid "Polyploid") species of the genus _[Coffea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea "Coffea")_, as it carries four copies of the eleven chromosomes (44 total) instead of the 2 copies of diploid species. Specifically, _Coffea arabica_ is itself the result of a hybridization between the diploids _[Coffea canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_ and _Coffea eugenioides_[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-14),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-15) thus making it an [allotetraploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotetraploid "Allotetraploid"), with _two_ copies of two different genomes. This hybridization event at the origin of _Coffea arabica_ is estimated between 1.08 million and 543,000 years ago and is linked to changing environmental conditions in East Africa.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-17)

## Distribution and habitat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Distribution and habitat")]

Endemic to the southwestern [highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands "Ethiopian Highlands") of [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Martinez-Torres-2006-18)_Coffea arabica_ is grown in dozens of countries between the [Tropic of Capricorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Capricorn "Tropic of Capricorn") and the [Tropic of Cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Cancer "Tropic of Cancer").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-19) It is commonly used as an [understory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understory "Understory") shrub. It has also been recovered from the [Boma Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boma_Plateau "Boma Plateau") in [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"). _Coffea arabica_ is also found on Mount [Marsabit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsabit "Marsabit") in northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), but it is unclear whether this is a truly native or naturalised occurrence; recent studies support it being naturalised.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-IUCN-21) The species is widely naturalised in areas outside its native land, in many parts of [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and assorted islands in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Islands "Caribbean Islands") and in the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islands "Pacific Islands").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-22)

Arabica coffee typically grows at high elevations with moderate temperatures and well drained soils.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-23)The species thrives in tropical climates with consistent rainfall and partial shade.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-24)The native habitat is characterized by montane forest with rich biodiversity.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-25)

The coffee tree was first brought to [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") in 1813, and it began to be extensively grown by about 1850.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-hawaii-26) It was formerly more widely grown, especially in [Kona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kona_District,_Hawaii "Kona District, Hawaii"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-hawaii-26) and it persists after cultivation in many areas. In some valleys, it is a highly invasive weed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-27) In the [Udawattakele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udawatta_Kele_Sanctuary "Udawatta Kele Sanctuary") and Gannoruwa Forest Reserves near Kandy, Sri Lanka, coffee shrubs are also a problematic invasive species.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-28)

In Hawaii, coffee cultivation became a major agricultural activity in the 19th century.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-29)However, escaped plants have spread beyond plantations and established wild populations. These populations can alter native ecosystems by competing with local plant species.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-30)

Coffee has been produced in Queensland and New South Wales of Australia, starting in the 1980s and 1990s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-31) The [Wet Tropics Management Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wet_Tropics_Management_Authority "Wet Tropics Management Authority") has classified _Coffea arabica_ as an environmental weed for southeast Queensland due to its invasiveness in non-agricultural areas.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-33)

Coffee production in Australia remains relatively small but has expanded in subtropical regions. Environmental concerns have arisen due to its ability to spread into surrounding natural habitats.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-34) Management efforts focus on limiting its spread outside cultivated areas.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-35)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_coffee "History of coffee")

The first written record of coffee made from [roasted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roasted "Roasted") coffee beans (botanical seeds) comes from [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab "Arab") scholars, who wrote that it was useful in prolonging their working hours. [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia") were likely pioneering regions for coffee bean cultivation.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-tuch-36) The Arab innovation in Yemen of making a brew from roasted beans spread first among the [Hijazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [Egyptians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and [Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_people "Turkish people"), and later found its way around the world. Some scholars believe that the coffee plant was introduced from Yemen, based on a Yemeni tradition that slips of both coffee and _[qat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catha\_edulis "Catha edulis")_ were planted at _Udein_ ('the two twigs') in Yemen in pre-Islamic times.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-tuch-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-37)[Arabica coffee production in Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabica_coffee_production_in_Indonesia "Arabica coffee production in Indonesia") began in 1699 through the spread of Yemen's trade. [Indonesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") coffees, such as [Sumatran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra") and Java, are known for their heavy body and low acidity. These qualities make them ideal for blending with the higher acidity coffees from [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Martinez-Torres-2006-18)

## Cultivation and use

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cultivation and use")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker%2C_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg/250px-Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker%2C_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker,_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg)

Botanical drawing of _Coffea arabica_, around 1860

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png/250px-Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png)

Botanical drawing of _C. arabica_, dating from around 1880

_Coffea arabica_ accounts for 60% of the world's coffee production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-CoffeeProduction-2)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-38)

_C. arabica_ takes approximately seven years to mature fully, and it does best with 1.2–1.8 metres (47–71 in) of rain, evenly distributed throughout the year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-40) It is usually cultivated at an altitude between 1,200 and 1,500 m (3,900 and 4,900 ft),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-41) but there are plantations that grow it as low as sea level and as high as 2,800 m (9,200 ft).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Schmitt2006-42)

The plant can tolerate low temperatures, but not frost, and it does best with an average temperature between 15 and 24°C (59 and 75°F).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Obso2006-43) Commercial [cultivars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivar "Cultivar") mostly only grow to about 5 m, and are frequently trimmed as low as 2 m to facilitate harvesting. Unlike _[Coffea canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_, _C. arabica_ prefers to be grown in light shade.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-44)

Three to four years after planting, _C. arabica_ produces small, white, highly fragrant flowers. The sweet fragrance resembles the sweet smell of [jasmine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasmine "Jasmine") flowers.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-45) Flowers opening on sunny days result in the greatest number of berries. This can be problematic and deleterious, however, as coffee plants tend to produce too many berries; this can lead to an inferior harvest and even damage yield in the following years, as the plant will favour the ripening of berries to the detriment of its vegetative growth.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-46)

On well-kept plantations, overflowering is prevented by pruning the tree. The flowers last only a few days, leaving behind only the thick, dark-green leaves. The berries then begin to appear.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-47) These are as dark green as the foliage until they begin to ripen, but as chlorophyll degrades and anthocyanins buildup, the plant becomes completely red or yellow depending on the variety of _C. arabica_. At this point, they are called "[cherries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherries "Cherries")", which fruit they then resemble, and are ready for picking.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-48)

The berries are oblong and about 1 cm long. Inferior coffee results from picking them too early or too late, so many are picked by hand to be able to better select them, as they do not all ripen at the same time.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-49) They are sometimes shaken off the tree onto mats, which means ripe and unripe berries are collected together.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-50)

The trees are difficult to cultivate and each tree can produce from 0.5 to 5.0 kilograms (1.1 to 11.0 lb) of dried beans, depending on the tree's individual character and the climate that season. The most valuable part of this [cash crop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_crop "Cash crop") is the beans inside. Each berry holds two [locules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locule "Locule") containing the beans. The coffee beans are actually two seeds within the fruit; sometimes, a third seed or one seed, a [peaberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peaberry "Peaberry"), grows in the fruit at the tips of the branches. These seeds are covered in two membranes; the outer one is called the "parchment coat" and the inner one is called the "silver skin".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-51)

On [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(island) "Java (island)"), trees are planted at all times of the year and are harvested year-round. In parts of [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), however, the trees have a season and are harvested only in winter. The plants are vulnerable to damage in such poor growing conditions as cold or [low pH soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_pH "Soil pH"), and they are also more vulnerable to pests than the _[C. robusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_ plant.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-52)

It is expected that a medium-term depletion of indigenous populations of _C. arabica_ may occur, due to projected [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming"), based on [IPCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_Panel_on_Climate_Change "Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change") modelling.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-53) Climate change—rising temperatures, longer droughts, and excessive rainfall—appears to threaten the sustainability of arabica coffee production, leading to attempts to breed new cultivars for the changing conditions[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-54).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-55)

Gourmet coffees are almost exclusively high-quality mild varieties of arabica coffee, and among the best known arabica coffee beans in the world are those from [Jamaican Blue Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Blue_Mountain_Coffee "Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee"), [Colombian Supremo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_coffee "Colombian coffee"), [Tarrazú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrazu_coffee "Tarrazu coffee"), [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"), [Guatemalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala")[Antigua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), and [Ethiopian Sidamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Sidamo_(coffee) "Ethiopian Sidamo (coffee)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-58)

Blends consisting only of Arabica are often labelled "100% Arabica" as a sign of quality. In 2023, several large coffee roasters dropped the "100% Arabica" declaration previously residing on some of their packages and started to blend less expensive [Robusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robusta "Robusta") coffee into the mix. To avoid making larger changes to the visual design of the package the Arabica label was replaced by other labeling, keeping the previous ornamental design, thereby presenting a case of [shrinkflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrinkflation "Shrinkflation"). In some case, the coffee is still advertised as "100% Arabica" in flyers in 2024, but is no longer declared so on the actual package.

## Strains

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Strains")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg/250px-Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg)

Structure of coffee berry and beans:  
1: Center cut  
2: Bean ([endosperm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosperm "Endosperm"))  
3: Silver skin (testa, [epidermis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidermis_(botany) "Epidermis (botany)"))  
4: Parchment coat (hull, [endocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocarp "Endocarp"))  
5: [Pectin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pectin "Pectin") layer  
6: Pulp ([mesocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesocarp "Mesocarp"))  
7: Outer skin ([pericarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericarp "Pericarp"), [exocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exocarp "Exocarp"))

One [strain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strain_(biology) "Strain (biology)") of _Coffea arabica_ (called AC1, AC2 and AC3 in honour of the geneticist Alcides Carvalho) naturally contains very little caffeine. While beans of normal _C. arabica_ plants contain 12 mg of caffeine per gram of dry mass, these mutants contain only 0.76 mg of caffeine per gram, with similar expected cup quality.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-59)

## Threats

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Threats")]

Although it has a huge wild population of 13.5 to 19.5 billion individuals throughout its native range, _C. arabica_ is still considered [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_species "Endangered species") on the [IUCN Red List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List "IUCN Red List") due to numerous threats it faces.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-60)Because it is an [understory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understory "Understory") plant, it needs standing forest, making it highly susceptible to the historically significant [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") levels in Ethiopia; before major deforestation, forest cover was thought to be between 25–31% of Ethiopia's total land surface, but has dropped to just 4%, and deforestation still continues.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-61) In addition, [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") may have a major effect on growing areas for wild _C. arabica_ in Ethiopia due to its high-temperature sensitivity, and estimates indicate that population could reduce by 50–80% with a 40–50% reduction in [area of occupancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_occupancy "Area of occupancy") by 2088[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-62); climate change can also impact reproductive success. In addition, the main pest of coffee, the [coffee berry borer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothenemus_hampei "Hypothenemus hampei") (_Hypothenemus hampei_) may benefit from climate change[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-63) and colonize higher altitudes that were formerly too cold for it, which can also affect coffee populations.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-IUCN-21)

Additionally, coffee leaf rust caused by the fungus _Hemileia vastatrix_ is a major threat to the supply of _Coffea arabica_ causing losses of up to $2 billion US dollars annually.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-64) From 2012 to 2013 _Hemileia vastatrix_ was responsible for a 16% decrease in production of _Coffea arabica_ across Central America. The fungus destroys the plant by causing rapid defoliation, which hinders the plant from performing photosynthesis.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-65)

The conservation of the genetic variation of _C. arabica_ relies on conserving healthy populations of wild coffee in the [Afromontane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afromontane "Afromontane")[rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforests "Rainforests") of Yemen. Genetic research has shown coffee [cultivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticulture "Horticulture") is threatening the genetic integrity of [wild coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_coffee "Wild coffee") because it exposes wild [genotypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genotypes "Genotypes") to [cultivars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivars "Cultivars")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-66).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-67) Nearly all of the coffee that has been cultivated over the past few centuries originated from just a handful of wild plants from Yemen, and the coffee growing on plantations around the world contains less than 1% of the diversity in the wilds of Yemen alone.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Saving_Coffee-68)

Climate change also serves as a threat to cultivated _C. arabica_ due to their temperature sensitivity, and some studies estimate that by 2050, over half of the land used for cultivating coffee could be unproductive. The more heat-tolerant _[Coffea stenophylla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_stenophylla "Coffea stenophylla")_ may replace _C. arabica_ as the dominant coffee species in cultivation in order to guard against this.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-69)

_**Coffea arabica**_ ([/ə ˈ r æ b ɪ k ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")), also known as the **Arabica coffee**, is a species of [flowering plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant "Flowering plant") in the [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and madder family [Rubiaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubiaceae "Rubiaceae"). It is believed to be the first species of coffee to have been cultivated and is the dominant cultivar, representing about 60% of global production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-CoffeeProduction-2) Coffee produced from the less acidic, more bitter, and more highly [caffeinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeinated "Caffeinated") robusta bean (_[C. canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_) makes up most of the remaining coffee production. The natural populations of _Coffea arabica_ are restricted to the forests of [South Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Ethiopia "South Ethiopia"), [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"), and [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-5)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

Wild plants grow between 9 and 12 m (30 and 39 ft) tall, and have an open branching system; the [leaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") are opposite, simple elliptic-ovate to oblong, 6–12 cm (2.5–4.5 in) long and 4–8 cm (1.5–3 in) broad, glossy dark green, with prominent veins and wavy margins.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-6)

The [flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower "Flower") are white, 10–15 mm in diameter, and grow in axillary clusters of 2 to 9. The fruit is a [drupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drupe "Drupe") (commonly called a "cherry") 10–15 mm in diameter, maturing bright red to purple and typically containing two [seeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seed "Seed") each which become [coffee beans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_bean "Coffee bean").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-8)

## Taxonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Taxonomy")]

The botanical name _Coffea arabica_ was formally published by [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") in his _[Species plantarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species\_plantarum "Species plantarum")_ in 1753.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-9) The species had been described and depicted before, as Linnaeus was able to refer to [Antoine de Jussieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_de_Jussieu "Antoine de Jussieu"), who named it _Jasminum arabicum_, published in 1715, after studying a specimen sent to him from the [Botanic Garden of Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hortus_Botanicus_(Amsterdam) "Hortus Botanicus (Amsterdam)"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-11)[Gaspard Bauhin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspard_Bauhin "Gaspard Bauhin")'s _Pinax_ of 1623 under 'Evonymus IV'[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-12) and [Prospero Alpini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospero_Alpini "Prospero Alpini")'s _De plantis Aegypti liber_, published in 1592.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-13)

_Coffea arabica_ is one of the [polyploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyploid "Polyploid") species of the genus _[Coffea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea "Coffea")_, as it carries four copies of the eleven chromosomes (44 total) instead of the 2 copies of diploid species. Specifically, _Coffea arabica_ is itself the result of a hybridization between the diploids _[Coffea canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_ and _Coffea eugenioides_[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-14),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-15) thus making it an [allotetraploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotetraploid "Allotetraploid"), with _two_ copies of two different genomes. This hybridization event at the origin of _Coffea arabica_ is estimated between 1.08 million and 543,000 years ago and is linked to changing environmental conditions in East Africa.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-17)

## Distribution and habitat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Distribution and habitat")]

Endemic to the southwestern [highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands "Ethiopian Highlands") of [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Martinez-Torres-2006-18)_Coffea arabica_ is grown in dozens of countries between the [Tropic of Capricorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Capricorn "Tropic of Capricorn") and the [Tropic of Cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Cancer "Tropic of Cancer").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-19) It is commonly used as an [understory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understory "Understory") shrub. It has also been recovered from the [Boma Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boma_Plateau "Boma Plateau") in [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"). _Coffea arabica_ is also found on Mount [Marsabit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsabit "Marsabit") in northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), but it is unclear whether this is a truly native or naturalised occurrence; recent studies support it being naturalised.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-IUCN-21) The species is widely naturalised in areas outside its native land, in many parts of [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and assorted islands in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Islands "Caribbean Islands") and in the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islands "Pacific Islands").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-22)

Arabica coffee typically grows at high elevations with moderate temperatures and well drained soils.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-23)The species thrives in tropical climates with consistent rainfall and partial shade.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-24)The native habitat is characterized by montane forest with rich biodiversity.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-25)

The coffee tree was first brought to [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") in 1813, and it began to be extensively grown by about 1850.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-hawaii-26) It was formerly more widely grown, especially in [Kona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kona_District,_Hawaii "Kona District, Hawaii"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-hawaii-26) and it persists after cultivation in many areas. In some valleys, it is a highly invasive weed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-27) In the [Udawattakele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udawatta_Kele_Sanctuary "Udawatta Kele Sanctuary") and Gannoruwa Forest Reserves near Kandy, Sri Lanka, coffee shrubs are also a problematic invasive species.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-28)

In Hawaii, coffee cultivation became a major agricultural activity in the 19th century.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-29)However, escaped plants have spread beyond plantations and established wild populations. These populations can alter native ecosystems by competing with local plant species.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-30)

Coffee has been produced in Queensland and New South Wales of Australia, starting in the 1980s and 1990s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-31) The [Wet Tropics Management Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wet_Tropics_Management_Authority "Wet Tropics Management Authority") has classified _Coffea arabica_ as an environmental weed for southeast Queensland due to its invasiveness in non-agricultural areas.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-33)

Coffee production in Australia remains relatively small but has expanded in subtropical regions. Environmental concerns have arisen due to its ability to spread into surrounding natural habitats.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-34) Management efforts focus on limiting its spread outside cultivated areas.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-35)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_coffee "History of coffee")

The first written record of coffee made from [roasted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roasted "Roasted") coffee beans (botanical seeds) comes from [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab "Arab") scholars, who wrote that it was useful in prolonging their working hours. [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia") were likely pioneering regions for coffee bean cultivation.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-tuch-36) The Arab innovation in Yemen of making a brew from roasted beans spread first among the [Hijazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [Egyptians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and [Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_people "Turkish people"), and later found its way around the world. Some scholars believe that the coffee plant was introduced from Yemen, based on a Yemeni tradition that slips of both coffee and _[qat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catha\_edulis "Catha edulis")_ were planted at _Udein_ ('the two twigs') in Yemen in pre-Islamic times.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-tuch-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-37)[Arabica coffee production in Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabica_coffee_production_in_Indonesia "Arabica coffee production in Indonesia") began in 1699 through the spread of Yemen's trade. [Indonesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") coffees, such as [Sumatran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra") and Java, are known for their heavy body and low acidity. These qualities make them ideal for blending with the higher acidity coffees from [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Martinez-Torres-2006-18)

## Cultivation and use

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cultivation and use")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker%2C_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg/250px-Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker%2C_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center_-_L.0939590_-_Bernecker,_A._-_Coffea_arabica_Linnaeus_-_Artwork.jpeg)

Botanical drawing of _Coffea arabica_, around 1860

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png/250px-Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coffea_arabica_Blanco1.53.png)

Botanical drawing of _C. arabica_, dating from around 1880

_Coffea arabica_ accounts for 60% of the world's coffee production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-CoffeeProduction-2)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-38)

_C. arabica_ takes approximately seven years to mature fully, and it does best with 1.2–1.8 metres (47–71 in) of rain, evenly distributed throughout the year.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-40) It is usually cultivated at an altitude between 1,200 and 1,500 m (3,900 and 4,900 ft),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-41) but there are plantations that grow it as low as sea level and as high as 2,800 m (9,200 ft).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Schmitt2006-42)

The plant can tolerate low temperatures, but not frost, and it does best with an average temperature between 15 and 24°C (59 and 75°F).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Obso2006-43) Commercial [cultivars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivar "Cultivar") mostly only grow to about 5 m, and are frequently trimmed as low as 2 m to facilitate harvesting. Unlike _[Coffea canephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_, _C. arabica_ prefers to be grown in light shade.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-44)

Three to four years after planting, _C. arabica_ produces small, white, highly fragrant flowers. The sweet fragrance resembles the sweet smell of [jasmine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasmine "Jasmine") flowers.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-45) Flowers opening on sunny days result in the greatest number of berries. This can be problematic and deleterious, however, as coffee plants tend to produce too many berries; this can lead to an inferior harvest and even damage yield in the following years, as the plant will favour the ripening of berries to the detriment of its vegetative growth.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-46)

On well-kept plantations, overflowering is prevented by pruning the tree. The flowers last only a few days, leaving behind only the thick, dark-green leaves. The berries then begin to appear.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-47) These are as dark green as the foliage until they begin to ripen, but as chlorophyll degrades and anthocyanins buildup, the plant becomes completely red or yellow depending on the variety of _C. arabica_. At this point, they are called "[cherries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherries "Cherries")", which fruit they then resemble, and are ready for picking.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-48)

The berries are oblong and about 1 cm long. Inferior coffee results from picking them too early or too late, so many are picked by hand to be able to better select them, as they do not all ripen at the same time.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-49) They are sometimes shaken off the tree onto mats, which means ripe and unripe berries are collected together.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-50)

The trees are difficult to cultivate and each tree can produce from 0.5 to 5.0 kilograms (1.1 to 11.0 lb) of dried beans, depending on the tree's individual character and the climate that season. The most valuable part of this [cash crop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_crop "Cash crop") is the beans inside. Each berry holds two [locules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locule "Locule") containing the beans. The coffee beans are actually two seeds within the fruit; sometimes, a third seed or one seed, a [peaberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peaberry "Peaberry"), grows in the fruit at the tips of the branches. These seeds are covered in two membranes; the outer one is called the "parchment coat" and the inner one is called the "silver skin".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-51)

On [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(island) "Java (island)"), trees are planted at all times of the year and are harvested year-round. In parts of [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), however, the trees have a season and are harvested only in winter. The plants are vulnerable to damage in such poor growing conditions as cold or [low pH soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_pH "Soil pH"), and they are also more vulnerable to pests than the _[C. robusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_canephora "Coffea canephora")_ plant.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-52)

It is expected that a medium-term depletion of indigenous populations of _C. arabica_ may occur, due to projected [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming"), based on [IPCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_Panel_on_Climate_Change "Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change") modelling.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-53) Climate change—rising temperatures, longer droughts, and excessive rainfall—appears to threaten the sustainability of arabica coffee production, leading to attempts to breed new cultivars for the changing conditions[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-54).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-55)

Gourmet coffees are almost exclusively high-quality mild varieties of arabica coffee, and among the best known arabica coffee beans in the world are those from [Jamaican Blue Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Blue_Mountain_Coffee "Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee"), [Colombian Supremo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_coffee "Colombian coffee"), [Tarrazú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrazu_coffee "Tarrazu coffee"), [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"), [Guatemalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala")[Antigua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), and [Ethiopian Sidamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Sidamo_(coffee) "Ethiopian Sidamo (coffee)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-58)

Blends consisting only of Arabica are often labelled "100% Arabica" as a sign of quality. In 2023, several large coffee roasters dropped the "100% Arabica" declaration previously residing on some of their packages and started to blend less expensive [Robusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robusta "Robusta") coffee into the mix. To avoid making larger changes to the visual design of the package the Arabica label was replaced by other labeling, keeping the previous ornamental design, thereby presenting a case of [shrinkflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrinkflation "Shrinkflation"). In some case, the coffee is still advertised as "100% Arabica" in flyers in 2024, but is no longer declared so on the actual package.

## Strains

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Strains")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg/250px-Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coffee_Bean_Structure.svg)

Structure of coffee berry and beans:  
1: Center cut  
2: Bean ([endosperm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosperm "Endosperm"))  
3: Silver skin (testa, [epidermis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidermis_(botany) "Epidermis (botany)"))  
4: Parchment coat (hull, [endocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocarp "Endocarp"))  
5: [Pectin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pectin "Pectin") layer  
6: Pulp ([mesocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesocarp "Mesocarp"))  
7: Outer skin ([pericarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericarp "Pericarp"), [exocarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exocarp "Exocarp"))

One [strain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strain_(biology) "Strain (biology)") of _Coffea arabica_ (called AC1, AC2 and AC3 in honour of the geneticist Alcides Carvalho) naturally contains very little caffeine. While beans of normal _C. arabica_ plants contain 12 mg of caffeine per gram of dry mass, these mutants contain only 0.76 mg of caffeine per gram, with similar expected cup quality.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-59)

## Threats

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coffea_arabica&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Threats")]

Although it has a huge wild population of 13.5 to 19.5 billion individuals throughout its native range, _C. arabica_ is still considered [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_species "Endangered species") on the [IUCN Red List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List "IUCN Red List") due to numerous threats it faces.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-60)Because it is an [understory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understory "Understory") plant, it needs standing forest, making it highly susceptible to the historically significant [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") levels in Ethiopia; before major deforestation, forest cover was thought to be between 25–31% of Ethiopia's total land surface, but has dropped to just 4%, and deforestation still continues.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-61) In addition, [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") may have a major effect on growing areas for wild _C. arabica_ in Ethiopia due to its high-temperature sensitivity, and estimates indicate that population could reduce by 50–80% with a 40–50% reduction in [area of occupancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_occupancy "Area of occupancy") by 2088[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-62); climate change can also impact reproductive success. In addition, the main pest of coffee, the [coffee berry borer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothenemus_hampei "Hypothenemus hampei") (_Hypothenemus hampei_) may benefit from climate change[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-63) and colonize higher altitudes that were formerly too cold for it, which can also affect coffee populations.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-IUCN-21)

Additionally, coffee leaf rust caused by the fungus _Hemileia vastatrix_ is a major threat to the supply of _Coffea arabica_ causing losses of up to $2 billion US dollars annually.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-64) From 2012 to 2013 _Hemileia vastatrix_ was responsible for a 16% decrease in production of _Coffea arabica_ across Central America. The fungus destroys the plant by causing rapid defoliation, which hinders the plant from performing photosynthesis.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-65)

The conservation of the genetic variation of _C. arabica_ relies on conserving healthy populations of wild coffee in the [Afromontane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afromontane "Afromontane")[rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforests "Rainforests") of Yemen. Genetic research has shown coffee [cultivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticulture "Horticulture") is threatening the genetic integrity of [wild coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_coffee "Wild coffee") because it exposes wild [genotypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genotypes "Genotypes") to [cultivars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivars "Cultivars")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-66).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-67) Nearly all of the coffee that has been cultivated over the past few centuries originated from just a handful of wild plants from Yemen, and the coffee growing on plantations around the world contains less than 1% of the diversity in the wilds of Yemen alone.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-Saving_Coffee-68)

Climate change also serves as a threat to cultivated _C. arabica_ due to their temperature sensitivity, and some studies estimate that by 2050, over half of the land used for cultivating coffee could be unproductive. The more heat-tolerant _[Coffea stenophylla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea\_stenophylla "Coffea stenophylla")_ may replace _C. arabica_ as the dominant coffee species in cultivation in order to guard against this.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffea_arabica#cite_note-69)

**Potosí**, known as **Villa Imperial de Potosí** in the colonial period, is the capital city and a municipality of the Department of Potosí in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). It is one of the [highest cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest_cities_in_the_world "List of highest cities in the world") in the world at a nominal 4,067 m (13,343 ft).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-3)[Diego Huallpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Huallpa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Diego Huallpa (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego%20Huallpa "es:Diego Huallpa")], an indigenous prospector, is traditionally credited with the discovery of the Cerro Rico in 1545,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-4) which led to the founding and rapid growth of Potosí due to its extraordinary silver wealth.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-5)

For centuries, it was the location of [the Spanish colonial silver mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mint_of_Bolivia "National Mint of Bolivia"). A considerable amount of the city's colonial architecture has been preserved in the historic center of the city, which—along with the globally important Cerro Rico de Potosí—are part of a designated UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Potosí lies at the foot of the _[Cerro de Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro\_Rico "Cerro Rico")_[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-6)—sometimes referred to as the _Cerro Rico_ ("rich mountain")—a [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") popularly conceived of as being "made of" [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") ore that dominates the city. The Cerro Rico is the reason for Potosí's historical importance since it was the major supply of silver for the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") until [Guanajuato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanajuato_City "Guanajuato City") in [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") surpassed it in the 18th century. At the turn of the 16th/17th centuries, it was the second largest city in the world, after London.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-7)[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Potos%C3%AD#Dubious "Talk:Potosí")_]

The silver was taken by [llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama "Llama") and [mule train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule_train_(transport) "Mule train (transport)") to the Pacific coast, shipped north to [Panama City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City "Panama City"), and carried by mule train across the isthmus of Panama to [Nombre de Dios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nombre_de_Dios,_Col%C3%B3n "Nombre de Dios, Colón") or [Portobelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portobelo,_Col%C3%B3n "Portobelo, Colón"), whence it was taken to Spain on the [Spanish treasure fleets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleets "Spanish treasure fleets"). Some of the silver also made its way east to [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), via the [Rio de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_de_la_Plata "Río de la Plata"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-8) or to [Acapulco, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acapulco,_Mexico "Acapulco, Mexico"), where it was sent via the [Manila Galleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Galleons "Manila Galleons") to buy Asian products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Schurz-9) Cerro de Potosí's peak is 4,824 m (15,827 ft)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):376

Today, Potosí continues to be an important mining center, and is the largest urban center in the Department of Potosí. A growing city, Potosí is now famous for its well-preserved colonial architecture, and unusual geographic setting as one of the highest cities in the world. It features a rare cold highland climate, and is marked by its long dry period, and short but strong wet season. While famous for its dominance as a mining center in early Spanish colonial history, Potosí still sits at one of the largest silver deposit systems in the world.
