A Spanish colonial two-reales piece ("two bits") from the Potosí Mint

There is no authoritative etymology for the word _Potosí_. According to legend, in about 1462, [Huayna Capac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac "Huayna Capac"), the eleventh [Sapa Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapa_Inca "Sapa Inca") of what by then was known as the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire") "set out for Ccolque Porco and Andaccaua, the location of his mines from which were taken innumerable [arrobas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arroba "Arroba") of silver" (an arroba is a Spanish unit of weight equivalent to approximately 25 lb (11 kg)). Before leaving there, he saw Potosí, and admiring its beauty and grandeur, he said (speaking to those of his Court):[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-12)

> "This doubtless must have much silver in its heart"; whereby he subsequently ordered his vassals to go to Ccolque Porco ... and work the mines and remove from them all the rich metal. They did so, and having brought their tools of flint and reinforced wood, they climbed the hill; and after having probed for its veins, they were about to open those veins when they heard a frightening thunderous noise which shook the whole hill, and after this, they heard a voice which said: "Do not take the silver from this hill, because it is destined for other masters." Amazed at hearing this reasoning, the Incan vassals desisted in their purpose and returned to Porco and told the king what had happened; relating the occurrence in their own language, on coming to the word noise, they said "Potocsí" which means there was a great thunderous noise, and from that later was derived (corrupting a letter) the name of Potosí.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

It is believed[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] that _Potosí_ is a [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") word.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] However, in Quechua the root _p'otoj_ does not refer to a thunderous noise, whereas it does in [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"). Thus, if _Potosí_ encompasses the idea of a thunderous noise, the location would have an Aymaran root rather than a Quechuan.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-14)

The actual sharp structure of the term is contrary to the nature of both Aymara and Quechua. Another explanation, given by several Quechua speakers,[_[specify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] is that _potoq_ is an [onomatopoeic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeic "Onomatopoeic") word that reproduces the sound of the hammer against the ore, and oral tradition has it that the town derived its name from this word.

### Colonial silver boom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Colonial silver boom")]

See also: [Real Situado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Situado "Real Situado") and [Global silver trade from the 16th to 18th centuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_silver_trade_from_the_16th_to_18th_centuries "Global silver trade from the 16th to 18th centuries")

Founded in 1545 as a mining town, it soon produced fabulous wealth, and the population eventually exceeded 200,000 people. The city gave rise to a [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") expression, still in use: _valer un Potosí_ ("to be worth a Potosí"), meaning "to be of great value". The rich mountain, [Cerro Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico"), produced an estimated 60% of all silver mined in the world during the second half of the 16th century.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:0-21)

Potosí miners at first mined the rich oxidized ores with [native silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_silver "Native silver") and silver chloride ([cerargyrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerargyrite "Cerargyrite")) that could be fed directly into smelting furnaces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:1-22) Especially successful were the small clay "flower pot" furnaces called _guayras_, which had been used by the Incas. By 1565, the miners had exhausted the direct-smelting ore, and silver production plummeted. Silver production was revived by the introduction of the [patio process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patio_process "Patio process"), invented by Spanish merchant [Bartolomé de Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolom%C3%A9_de_Medina_(mining_specialist) "Bartolomé de Medina (mining specialist)") in 1554. The patio process used mercury amalgamation to extract silver from lower-grade ores, and those containing silver sulfide ([argentite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentite "Argentite")), as was typical of the unoxidized ores found deeper in the mountain. In 1609, another mercury amalgamation method, the [pan amalgamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_amalgamation "Pan amalgamation") process was invented in Potosí, and proved better-adapted to the conditions at Potosí.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-23)

Spanish American mines were the world's most abundant sources of silver during this time period. Spanish America's ability to supply a great amount of silver and China's strong demand for this commodity which the Spanish supplied via Latin American trade with the Philippines using the [Manila Galleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Galleons "Manila Galleons"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Schurz-9) resulted in a spectacular mining boom. The true champion of this boom in the silver industry was indeed the Spanish crown. By allowing private-sector entrepreneurs to operate mines under license and placing high taxes on mining profits, the Spanish empire was able to extract the greatest benefits. An example of a tax that was levied includes the _quinto_, a 20% severance tax on gross value.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:0-21) From the raw materials extracted from the mines, coins called [pieces of eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_dollar "Spanish dollar") were fashioned at the Potosí mint.

For Europeans, Peru–[Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") was located in the [Viceroyalty of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_Peru "Viceroyalty of Peru") and was known as "[Upper Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Peru "Upper Peru")" before becoming independent as part of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Potosí was a mythical land of riches, it is mentioned in [Miguel de Cervantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes "Miguel de Cervantes")' famous novel, _[Don Quixote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don\_Quixote "Don Quixote")_ (second part, chap. LXXI) as a land of "extraordinary richness". One theory holds that the [mint mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_mark "Mint mark") of Potosí (the letters "PTSI" superimposed on one another) is the origin of the [dollar sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_sign#Potosi_mint_mark "Dollar sign").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The urban complex in the remote Andes was important enough to be designated a _Villa Imperial_ in the hierarchy of Spanish urban settlements. Although in mountainous terrain, the core of Potosí was laid out in the standard Spanish grid pattern, while the _rancherias_ (Indigenous settlements on the northern flank of the Cerro Rico) were more haphazard. According to an anonymous description of the city, by 1603 some 6,000 Spaniards and other Europeans, 5,000 Africans, an unspecified number of people of mixed heritage and at least 120,000 native Andeans were resident in Potosi. The villa was governed by a Spanish [corregidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corregidor_(position) "Corregidor (position)"), 2 [Alcaldes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcalde "Alcalde") and a town council of 19 men. At this time, it was the second largest city in the world, after London.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-24)

In addition to five publicly employed scribes, some forty independent notaries documented and recorded commercial transactions as well as last wills and testaments. Since Potosí was of such economic importance to the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), the crown bureaucracy was a significant presence. Large churches, lavishly decorated inside, were built, and friars from the Dominican, Franciscans, Augustinians, Mercederians, and Jesuits were present, but no convent for women existed until 1650. There was an ecclesiastical court for legal issues regarding the clergy. The [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition "Spanish Inquisition") had no tribunal in the city, but relied on a commissioner.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-25)

### Labor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Labor")]

Indigenous laborers were required to work in Potosí's silver mines through the Spanish _[mita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mit'a#Spanish\_rule "Mit'a")_ system of forced labor, based on an analogous _[mit'a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mit'a "Mit'a")_ system traditional to pre-Hispanic Andean society (though the _mit'a_ directed labor for public works and collective agricultural projects).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-26) Laborers were drawn from the native population of an area that encompassed almost 200,000 square miles.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-27) Thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year, constituting about one out of every seven adult males in the indigenous population.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-28) These _mitayos_ faced harsh conditions in the mines, where they were often given the least desirable jobs. While more skilled laborers extracted the ore, _mitayos_ were tasked with carrying it back to the surface in baskets, leather bags, or cloth sacks.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Burkholder_and_Johnson,_155-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30)

These loads often weighed between 100 and 300 lbs, and the workers had to carry them up rickety ladders in steep, narrow shafts lit only by a candle tied to their foreheads.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Burkholder_and_Johnson,_155-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30) Many of them died or were seriously injured due to falls, accidents, and the harsh conditions of the mine life. Illness was another danger: at such a high altitude, pneumonia was always a concern, especially given the extreme and rapid changes of temperature experienced by workers climbing from the heat of the deep shafts to the freezing elements of the surface at 16,000 feet, and mercury poisoning took the lives of many[_[quantify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] involved in the refining process.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30)

The Potosí _mita_ caused dramatic demographic shifts in the local indigenous population as wives and children moved with workers to Potosí while thousands more fled their traditional villages, forfeiting their _[ayllu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayllu "Ayllu")_ land rights in order to escape the labor draft.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-32) In rough terms the area affected by these displacements went from [Quito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quito "Quito") to [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-choquemari%C3%B1o-33) By the late 17th century, upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its indigenous population compared to a little over a century earlier.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-34) This only increased the burden on the remaining natives, and at some point in the 1600s, up to half of the eligible male population might find themselves working at Potosí. Nevertheless, the number of _mitayos_ dropped to about 4,000 by 1689, prompting the Viceroy [Duke of Palata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melchor_de_Navarra,_Duke_of_Palata "Melchor de Navarra, Duke of Palata") to raise the number again through a new census and inclusion of new populations not subject to the mita (_forasteros_).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-35) It is suspected that Spanish authorities in [Arica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arica "Arica"), [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre "Sucre") and [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro "Oruro") may not have responded to calls by Potosí authorities to locate escapees since many of these had proved useful workforce in agricultural [haciendas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") of influential Spaniards.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-choquemari%C3%B1o-33)

The reform failed, and the Duke's successor set the official number to 4,108 mitayos (1,367 active each week). In reality, the number of _mitayos_ was even lower due to the increasing practice of buying oneself out of the obligation. For the remaining mita workforce, however, conditions remained harsh. Mine and mill owners notoriously ignored official regulations on provisions and especially withheld the money the Indians should receive as recompensation for their travel. Just the cost of traveling to Potosí and back could be more than a _mitayo_ was paid in a year, and so many of them chose to remain in Potosí as wage workers when their _mita_ was finished.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_125-36) Former _mitayos_ living in Potosí were not only exempt from the draft, but usually earned considerably more due to the valuable skills they had gained in permanent services.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-37)

According to historian [Noble David Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_David_Cook "Noble David Cook"), "A key factor in understanding the impact of the Potosi mita on the Indians is that mita labor was only one form of work at the mines. A 1603 report stated that of 58,800 Indians working at Potosi, 5100 were _mitayos_, or fewer than one in ten. In addition to the mitayos there were 10,500 _mingas_ (contractual workers) and 43,200 free wage earners."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-38) However, historian Peter Bakewell emphasizes the role of mita labor in Potosí to a greater extent. According to his research, though as few as 4500 _mitayos_ were actively laboring in the mines at any given time, this was due to the _mita ordinaria_ system, in which the up to 13,500 men conscripted per year were divided into three parts, each working one out of every three weeks.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_125-36) In addition, many of the remaining _mingas_ and wage workers were either _mita ordinaria_ workers on their off weeks or former _mitayos_ who remained in Potosí.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-39)

Within the mines, a figure called el Tío acts as a deity of the land itself. El Tío serves as a figure of the mountain itself. Laborers within the mines offer coca leaves and alcohol to statues constructed within the mines of the deity to protect themselves from the dangerous conditions.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-40)

### Colonial-era society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Colonial-era society")]

Potosí was a multiracial society, with native Andeans, Spanish settlers, and black slaves.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:1-22) The largest sector of the population were native men, forced to labor underground mining the silver ore, but there were considerable opportunities for merchants and native traders, who became wealthy. Suppliers of food as well as holders of urban and rural real estate prospered in Potosí. Women, particularly widows, held property, since they were guaranteed a portion of their husband's estate under Spanish law. Small-scale female vendors dominated street markets and stalls, selling food, [coca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca "Coca") leaves, and [chicha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicha "Chicha") (maize beer).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-41) A portion of the female population were sex workers, who worked in brothels, many of which were annexed to gambling dens.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-42)

In the early 17th century, [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Basques#Modern_period "History of the Basques") were well established in the city and made up for a substantial number of the inhabitants in Potosí. They gathered in a confederation opposed to another one, the _Vicuñas_, a melting pot of natives and non-Basque Spanish and Portuguese colonists, fighting for control over ore extraction from the mines and its management. Eventually, tension among both factions came to a head, resulting in the eruption of [overt armed conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Vicu%C3%B1as_and_Basques "War of the Vicuñas and Basques") starting 1622 up to 1625. The Spanish Crown intervened, siding at one point with the Basques. Both factions reached a settlement sealed with a wedding between the son and daughter of the leaders in either side, the Basque Francisco Oyanume and the Vicuña general Castillo. One of the most famous Basque residents in Potosí (1617–19) was [Catalina de Erauso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalina_de_Erauso "Catalina de Erauso"), a nun who escaped her convent and dressed as a man, becoming a driver of llamas and a soldier.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-43)

### Independence era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independence era")]

During the [Bolivian War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_War_of_Independence "Bolivian War of Independence") (1809–1825), Potosí frequently passed between the control of Royalist and Patriot forces. Major leadership mistakes came when the First Auxiliary Army arrived from [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires") (under the command of [Juan José Castelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Jos%C3%A9_Castelli "Juan José Castelli")), which led to an increased sense that Potosí required its own independent government.

Later,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the Second Auxiliary Army (under the command of [Manuel Belgrano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Belgrano "Manuel Belgrano")) was forced to retreat, Belgrano made the decision to blow up the [Casa de la Moneda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_la_Moneda_de_Bolivia "Casa de la Moneda de Bolivia"). The natives undid the fuse, as many refused to evacuate and would have lost their lives. Two more expeditions from Buenos Aires would seize Potosí[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_].

### Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Geology")]

Located in the [Bolivian tin belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_tin_belt "Bolivian tin belt"), Cerro Rico de Potosí is the world's largest silver deposit and has been mined since the sixteenth century, producing up to 60,000 [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnes "Tonnes") by 1996. Estimates are that much silver still remains in the mines. Potosí became the second largest city, and the site of the first mint, in the Americas. By 1891, low silver prices prompted the change to mining tin, which continued until 1985. At peak production in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the [ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore "Ore") contained up to 40% silver.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):374

The ore deposits reside in [veins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vein_(geology) "Vein (geology)") present in the [dacite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacite "Dacite")[volcanic dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_dome "Volcanic dome"). The hill is "honeycombed" with underground workings, reaching from the summit to depths of 1,150 m (3,770 ft). The conical hill has a reddish-brown [gossan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossan "Gossan") cap of iron-oxides and quartz, with grayish-blue altered dacite and many [mine dumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_dump "Mine dump") below.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):374–376

[Basement rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basement_rock "Basement rock") consist of [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician")[clastic sediments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clastic_sediment "Clastic sediment") consisting of [phyllite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllite "Phyllite") with some [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone")[interbedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbedding "Interbedding"). At about 13.8 [Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myr "Myr"), the dome was [extruded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrusive_(geology) "Extrusive (geology)"). During the explosive process, the Venus [breccia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breccia "Breccia") formed when the ascending dacite [magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma "Magma") reacted with [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") to produce a [phreatic eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatic_eruption "Phreatic eruption"). The released pressure allowed the formation of the Caracoles [tuff ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff_ring "Tuff ring") on top of the breccia. The magma then extruded outward from a [dike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_(geology) "Dike (geology)") to form a [volcanic dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_dome "Volcanic dome") over the [tuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff "Tuff"). The dacite dome is 1,700 m (5,600 ft) by 1,200 m (3,900 ft) at the surface and narrows down to the 100 m (330 ft) wide dike at depth. [Hydrothermal circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_circulation "Hydrothermal circulation") and [fracturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fracture_(geology) "Fracture (geology)") soon followed, altering the dacite and depositing ore minerals and [gangue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangue "Gangue") in the veins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):375,381,384

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate")]

See also: [Rainy season in the Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainy_season_in_the_Altiplano "Rainy season in the Altiplano")

Potosí features a [cold subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate#Subpolar_oceanic_and_cold_subtropical_highland_varieties_(Cfc,_Cwc) "Oceanic climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _Cwc_, [Trewartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification "Trewartha climate classification"): _Eolk_). Summers are cool and wet, with daily highs rarely rising above 20°C (68°F). Winters have cooler days with much colder nights, averaging −4°C (25°F). These low temperatures are a result of the extreme precipitation deficit during the winter months, with the resulting aridity leading to an increased diurnal temperature variation.

## Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sports")]

Potosí is home to football teams [Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Potos%C3%AD "Real Potosí") and [Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacional_Potos%C3%AD "Nacional Potosí"), which play their matches at the 32,000-capacity multi-purpose stadium [Estadio Víctor Agustín Ugarte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_V%C3%ADctor_Agust%C3%ADn_Ugarte "Estadio Víctor Agustín Ugarte"), one of the highest stadiums in the world.

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Transportation")]

The city is served by [Aeropuerto Capitán Nicolas Rojas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Nicolas_Rojas_Airport "Captain Nicolas Rojas Airport"), with commercial airline flights by [Boliviana de Aviación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boliviana_de_Aviaci%C3%B3n "Boliviana de Aviación"), Bolivia's flag air carrier. There is also a railroad, the [Rio Mulatos-Potosí line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Mulatos-Potos%C3%AD_line "Rio Mulatos-Potosí line").

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Legacy")]

The city of [San Luis Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Luis_Potos%C3%AD_(city) "San Luis Potosí (city)") in Mexico was named after Potosí in Bolivia. In the United States, the name Potosi was optimistically given to lead-mining towns of [Potosi, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Wisconsin "Potosi, Wisconsin"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-49) and [Potosi, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Missouri "Potosi, Missouri"), and also to the silver-mining town of [Potosi, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Nevada "Potosi, Nevada").

**Potosí**, known as **Villa Imperial de Potosí** in the colonial period, is the capital city and a municipality of the Department of Potosí in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). It is one of the [highest cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest_cities_in_the_world "List of highest cities in the world") in the world at a nominal 4,067 m (13,343 ft).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-3)[Diego Huallpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Huallpa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Diego Huallpa (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego%20Huallpa "es:Diego Huallpa")], an indigenous prospector, is traditionally credited with the discovery of the Cerro Rico in 1545,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-4) which led to the founding and rapid growth of Potosí due to its extraordinary silver wealth.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-5)

For centuries, it was the location of [the Spanish colonial silver mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mint_of_Bolivia "National Mint of Bolivia"). A considerable amount of the city's colonial architecture has been preserved in the historic center of the city, which—along with the globally important Cerro Rico de Potosí—are part of a designated UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Potosí lies at the foot of the _[Cerro de Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro\_Rico "Cerro Rico")_[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-6)—sometimes referred to as the _Cerro Rico_ ("rich mountain")—a [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") popularly conceived of as being "made of" [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") ore that dominates the city. The Cerro Rico is the reason for Potosí's historical importance since it was the major supply of silver for the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") until [Guanajuato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanajuato_City "Guanajuato City") in [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") surpassed it in the 18th century. At the turn of the 16th/17th centuries, it was the second largest city in the world, after London.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-7)[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Potos%C3%AD#Dubious "Talk:Potosí")_]

The silver was taken by [llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama "Llama") and [mule train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule_train_(transport) "Mule train (transport)") to the Pacific coast, shipped north to [Panama City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City "Panama City"), and carried by mule train across the isthmus of Panama to [Nombre de Dios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nombre_de_Dios,_Col%C3%B3n "Nombre de Dios, Colón") or [Portobelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portobelo,_Col%C3%B3n "Portobelo, Colón"), whence it was taken to Spain on the [Spanish treasure fleets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleets "Spanish treasure fleets"). Some of the silver also made its way east to [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), via the [Rio de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_de_la_Plata "Río de la Plata"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-8) or to [Acapulco, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acapulco,_Mexico "Acapulco, Mexico"), where it was sent via the [Manila Galleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Galleons "Manila Galleons") to buy Asian products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Schurz-9) Cerro de Potosí's peak is 4,824 m (15,827 ft)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):376

Today, Potosí continues to be an important mining center, and is the largest urban center in the Department of Potosí. A growing city, Potosí is now famous for its well-preserved colonial architecture, and unusual geographic setting as one of the highest cities in the world. It features a rare cold highland climate, and is marked by its long dry period, and short but strong wet season. While famous for its dominance as a mining center in early Spanish colonial history, Potosí still sits at one of the largest silver deposit systems in the world.

There is no authoritative etymology for the word _Potosí_. According to legend, in about 1462, [Huayna Capac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac "Huayna Capac"), the eleventh [Sapa Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapa_Inca "Sapa Inca") of what by then was known as the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire") "set out for Ccolque Porco and Andaccaua, the location of his mines from which were taken innumerable [arrobas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arroba "Arroba") of silver" (an arroba is a Spanish unit of weight equivalent to approximately 25 lb (11 kg)). Before leaving there, he saw Potosí, and admiring its beauty and grandeur, he said (speaking to those of his Court):[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-12)

> "This doubtless must have much silver in its heart"; whereby he subsequently ordered his vassals to go to Ccolque Porco ... and work the mines and remove from them all the rich metal. They did so, and having brought their tools of flint and reinforced wood, they climbed the hill; and after having probed for its veins, they were about to open those veins when they heard a frightening thunderous noise which shook the whole hill, and after this, they heard a voice which said: "Do not take the silver from this hill, because it is destined for other masters." Amazed at hearing this reasoning, the Incan vassals desisted in their purpose and returned to Porco and told the king what had happened; relating the occurrence in their own language, on coming to the word noise, they said "Potocsí" which means there was a great thunderous noise, and from that later was derived (corrupting a letter) the name of Potosí.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

It is believed[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] that _Potosí_ is a [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") word.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] However, in Quechua the root _p'otoj_ does not refer to a thunderous noise, whereas it does in [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"). Thus, if _Potosí_ encompasses the idea of a thunderous noise, the location would have an Aymaran root rather than a Quechuan.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-14)

The actual sharp structure of the term is contrary to the nature of both Aymara and Quechua. Another explanation, given by several Quechua speakers,[_[specify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] is that _potoq_ is an [onomatopoeic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeic "Onomatopoeic") word that reproduces the sound of the hammer against the ore, and oral tradition has it that the town derived its name from this word.

### Colonial silver boom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Colonial silver boom")]

See also: [Real Situado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Situado "Real Situado") and [Global silver trade from the 16th to 18th centuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_silver_trade_from_the_16th_to_18th_centuries "Global silver trade from the 16th to 18th centuries")

Founded in 1545 as a mining town, it soon produced fabulous wealth, and the population eventually exceeded 200,000 people. The city gave rise to a [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") expression, still in use: _valer un Potosí_ ("to be worth a Potosí"), meaning "to be of great value". The rich mountain, [Cerro Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico "Cerro Rico"), produced an estimated 60% of all silver mined in the world during the second half of the 16th century.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:0-21)

Potosí miners at first mined the rich oxidized ores with [native silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_silver "Native silver") and silver chloride ([cerargyrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerargyrite "Cerargyrite")) that could be fed directly into smelting furnaces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:1-22) Especially successful were the small clay "flower pot" furnaces called _guayras_, which had been used by the Incas. By 1565, the miners had exhausted the direct-smelting ore, and silver production plummeted. Silver production was revived by the introduction of the [patio process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patio_process "Patio process"), invented by Spanish merchant [Bartolomé de Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolom%C3%A9_de_Medina_(mining_specialist) "Bartolomé de Medina (mining specialist)") in 1554. The patio process used mercury amalgamation to extract silver from lower-grade ores, and those containing silver sulfide ([argentite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentite "Argentite")), as was typical of the unoxidized ores found deeper in the mountain. In 1609, another mercury amalgamation method, the [pan amalgamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_amalgamation "Pan amalgamation") process was invented in Potosí, and proved better-adapted to the conditions at Potosí.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-23)

Spanish American mines were the world's most abundant sources of silver during this time period. Spanish America's ability to supply a great amount of silver and China's strong demand for this commodity which the Spanish supplied via Latin American trade with the Philippines using the [Manila Galleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Galleons "Manila Galleons"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Schurz-9) resulted in a spectacular mining boom. The true champion of this boom in the silver industry was indeed the Spanish crown. By allowing private-sector entrepreneurs to operate mines under license and placing high taxes on mining profits, the Spanish empire was able to extract the greatest benefits. An example of a tax that was levied includes the _quinto_, a 20% severance tax on gross value.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:0-21) From the raw materials extracted from the mines, coins called [pieces of eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_dollar "Spanish dollar") were fashioned at the Potosí mint.

For Europeans, Peru–[Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") was located in the [Viceroyalty of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_Peru "Viceroyalty of Peru") and was known as "[Upper Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Peru "Upper Peru")" before becoming independent as part of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Potosí was a mythical land of riches, it is mentioned in [Miguel de Cervantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes "Miguel de Cervantes")' famous novel, _[Don Quixote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don\_Quixote "Don Quixote")_ (second part, chap. LXXI) as a land of "extraordinary richness". One theory holds that the [mint mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_mark "Mint mark") of Potosí (the letters "PTSI" superimposed on one another) is the origin of the [dollar sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_sign#Potosi_mint_mark "Dollar sign").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The urban complex in the remote Andes was important enough to be designated a _Villa Imperial_ in the hierarchy of Spanish urban settlements. Although in mountainous terrain, the core of Potosí was laid out in the standard Spanish grid pattern, while the _rancherias_ (Indigenous settlements on the northern flank of the Cerro Rico) were more haphazard. According to an anonymous description of the city, by 1603 some 6,000 Spaniards and other Europeans, 5,000 Africans, an unspecified number of people of mixed heritage and at least 120,000 native Andeans were resident in Potosi. The villa was governed by a Spanish [corregidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corregidor_(position) "Corregidor (position)"), 2 [Alcaldes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcalde "Alcalde") and a town council of 19 men. At this time, it was the second largest city in the world, after London.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-24)

In addition to five publicly employed scribes, some forty independent notaries documented and recorded commercial transactions as well as last wills and testaments. Since Potosí was of such economic importance to the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), the crown bureaucracy was a significant presence. Large churches, lavishly decorated inside, were built, and friars from the Dominican, Franciscans, Augustinians, Mercederians, and Jesuits were present, but no convent for women existed until 1650. There was an ecclesiastical court for legal issues regarding the clergy. The [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition "Spanish Inquisition") had no tribunal in the city, but relied on a commissioner.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-25)

### Labor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Labor")]

Indigenous laborers were required to work in Potosí's silver mines through the Spanish _[mita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mit'a#Spanish\_rule "Mit'a")_ system of forced labor, based on an analogous _[mit'a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mit'a "Mit'a")_ system traditional to pre-Hispanic Andean society (though the _mit'a_ directed labor for public works and collective agricultural projects).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-26) Laborers were drawn from the native population of an area that encompassed almost 200,000 square miles.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-27) Thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year, constituting about one out of every seven adult males in the indigenous population.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-28) These _mitayos_ faced harsh conditions in the mines, where they were often given the least desirable jobs. While more skilled laborers extracted the ore, _mitayos_ were tasked with carrying it back to the surface in baskets, leather bags, or cloth sacks.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Burkholder_and_Johnson,_155-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30)

These loads often weighed between 100 and 300 lbs, and the workers had to carry them up rickety ladders in steep, narrow shafts lit only by a candle tied to their foreheads.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Burkholder_and_Johnson,_155-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30) Many of them died or were seriously injured due to falls, accidents, and the harsh conditions of the mine life. Illness was another danger: at such a high altitude, pneumonia was always a concern, especially given the extreme and rapid changes of temperature experienced by workers climbing from the heat of the deep shafts to the freezing elements of the surface at 16,000 feet, and mercury poisoning took the lives of many[_[quantify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] involved in the refining process.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_130-30)

The Potosí _mita_ caused dramatic demographic shifts in the local indigenous population as wives and children moved with workers to Potosí while thousands more fled their traditional villages, forfeiting their _[ayllu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayllu "Ayllu")_ land rights in order to escape the labor draft.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-32) In rough terms the area affected by these displacements went from [Quito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quito "Quito") to [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-choquemari%C3%B1o-33) By the late 17th century, upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its indigenous population compared to a little over a century earlier.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-34) This only increased the burden on the remaining natives, and at some point in the 1600s, up to half of the eligible male population might find themselves working at Potosí. Nevertheless, the number of _mitayos_ dropped to about 4,000 by 1689, prompting the Viceroy [Duke of Palata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melchor_de_Navarra,_Duke_of_Palata "Melchor de Navarra, Duke of Palata") to raise the number again through a new census and inclusion of new populations not subject to the mita (_forasteros_).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-35) It is suspected that Spanish authorities in [Arica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arica "Arica"), [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre "Sucre") and [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro "Oruro") may not have responded to calls by Potosí authorities to locate escapees since many of these had proved useful workforce in agricultural [haciendas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") of influential Spaniards.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-choquemari%C3%B1o-33)

The reform failed, and the Duke's successor set the official number to 4,108 mitayos (1,367 active each week). In reality, the number of _mitayos_ was even lower due to the increasing practice of buying oneself out of the obligation. For the remaining mita workforce, however, conditions remained harsh. Mine and mill owners notoriously ignored official regulations on provisions and especially withheld the money the Indians should receive as recompensation for their travel. Just the cost of traveling to Potosí and back could be more than a _mitayo_ was paid in a year, and so many of them chose to remain in Potosí as wage workers when their _mita_ was finished.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_125-36) Former _mitayos_ living in Potosí were not only exempt from the draft, but usually earned considerably more due to the valuable skills they had gained in permanent services.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-37)

According to historian [Noble David Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_David_Cook "Noble David Cook"), "A key factor in understanding the impact of the Potosi mita on the Indians is that mita labor was only one form of work at the mines. A 1603 report stated that of 58,800 Indians working at Potosi, 5100 were _mitayos_, or fewer than one in ten. In addition to the mitayos there were 10,500 _mingas_ (contractual workers) and 43,200 free wage earners."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-38) However, historian Peter Bakewell emphasizes the role of mita labor in Potosí to a greater extent. According to his research, though as few as 4500 _mitayos_ were actively laboring in the mines at any given time, this was due to the _mita ordinaria_ system, in which the up to 13,500 men conscripted per year were divided into three parts, each working one out of every three weeks.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Bakewell,_125-36) In addition, many of the remaining _mingas_ and wage workers were either _mita ordinaria_ workers on their off weeks or former _mitayos_ who remained in Potosí.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-39)

Within the mines, a figure called el Tío acts as a deity of the land itself. El Tío serves as a figure of the mountain itself. Laborers within the mines offer coca leaves and alcohol to statues constructed within the mines of the deity to protect themselves from the dangerous conditions.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-40)

### Colonial-era society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Colonial-era society")]

Potosí was a multiracial society, with native Andeans, Spanish settlers, and black slaves.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-:1-22) The largest sector of the population were native men, forced to labor underground mining the silver ore, but there were considerable opportunities for merchants and native traders, who became wealthy. Suppliers of food as well as holders of urban and rural real estate prospered in Potosí. Women, particularly widows, held property, since they were guaranteed a portion of their husband's estate under Spanish law. Small-scale female vendors dominated street markets and stalls, selling food, [coca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca "Coca") leaves, and [chicha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicha "Chicha") (maize beer).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-41) A portion of the female population were sex workers, who worked in brothels, many of which were annexed to gambling dens.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-42)

In the early 17th century, [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Basques#Modern_period "History of the Basques") were well established in the city and made up for a substantial number of the inhabitants in Potosí. They gathered in a confederation opposed to another one, the _Vicuñas_, a melting pot of natives and non-Basque Spanish and Portuguese colonists, fighting for control over ore extraction from the mines and its management. Eventually, tension among both factions came to a head, resulting in the eruption of [overt armed conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Vicu%C3%B1as_and_Basques "War of the Vicuñas and Basques") starting 1622 up to 1625. The Spanish Crown intervened, siding at one point with the Basques. Both factions reached a settlement sealed with a wedding between the son and daughter of the leaders in either side, the Basque Francisco Oyanume and the Vicuña general Castillo. One of the most famous Basque residents in Potosí (1617–19) was [Catalina de Erauso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalina_de_Erauso "Catalina de Erauso"), a nun who escaped her convent and dressed as a man, becoming a driver of llamas and a soldier.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-43)

### Independence era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independence era")]

During the [Bolivian War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_War_of_Independence "Bolivian War of Independence") (1809–1825), Potosí frequently passed between the control of Royalist and Patriot forces. Major leadership mistakes came when the First Auxiliary Army arrived from [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires") (under the command of [Juan José Castelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Jos%C3%A9_Castelli "Juan José Castelli")), which led to an increased sense that Potosí required its own independent government.

Later,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the Second Auxiliary Army (under the command of [Manuel Belgrano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Belgrano "Manuel Belgrano")) was forced to retreat, Belgrano made the decision to blow up the [Casa de la Moneda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_la_Moneda_de_Bolivia "Casa de la Moneda de Bolivia"). The natives undid the fuse, as many refused to evacuate and would have lost their lives. Two more expeditions from Buenos Aires would seize Potosí[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_].

### Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Geology")]

Located in the [Bolivian tin belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_tin_belt "Bolivian tin belt"), Cerro Rico de Potosí is the world's largest silver deposit and has been mined since the sixteenth century, producing up to 60,000 [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnes "Tonnes") by 1996. Estimates are that much silver still remains in the mines. Potosí became the second largest city, and the site of the first mint, in the Americas. By 1891, low silver prices prompted the change to mining tin, which continued until 1985. At peak production in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the [ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore "Ore") contained up to 40% silver.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):374

The ore deposits reside in [veins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vein_(geology) "Vein (geology)") present in the [dacite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacite "Dacite")[volcanic dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_dome "Volcanic dome"). The hill is "honeycombed" with underground workings, reaching from the summit to depths of 1,150 m (3,770 ft). The conical hill has a reddish-brown [gossan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossan "Gossan") cap of iron-oxides and quartz, with grayish-blue altered dacite and many [mine dumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_dump "Mine dump") below.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):374–376

[Basement rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basement_rock "Basement rock") consist of [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician")[clastic sediments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clastic_sediment "Clastic sediment") consisting of [phyllite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllite "Phyllite") with some [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone")[interbedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbedding "Interbedding"). At about 13.8 [Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myr "Myr"), the dome was [extruded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrusive_(geology) "Extrusive (geology)"). During the explosive process, the Venus [breccia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breccia "Breccia") formed when the ascending dacite [magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma "Magma") reacted with [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") to produce a [phreatic eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatic_eruption "Phreatic eruption"). The released pressure allowed the formation of the Caracoles [tuff ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff_ring "Tuff ring") on top of the breccia. The magma then extruded outward from a [dike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_(geology) "Dike (geology)") to form a [volcanic dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_dome "Volcanic dome") over the [tuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff "Tuff"). The dacite dome is 1,700 m (5,600 ft) by 1,200 m (3,900 ft) at the surface and narrows down to the 100 m (330 ft) wide dike at depth. [Hydrothermal circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_circulation "Hydrothermal circulation") and [fracturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fracture_(geology) "Fracture (geology)") soon followed, altering the dacite and depositing ore minerals and [gangue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangue "Gangue") in the veins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-Cunningham-10):375,381,384

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate")]

See also: [Rainy season in the Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainy_season_in_the_Altiplano "Rainy season in the Altiplano")

Potosí features a [cold subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate#Subpolar_oceanic_and_cold_subtropical_highland_varieties_(Cfc,_Cwc) "Oceanic climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _Cwc_, [Trewartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification "Trewartha climate classification"): _Eolk_). Summers are cool and wet, with daily highs rarely rising above 20°C (68°F). Winters have cooler days with much colder nights, averaging −4°C (25°F). These low temperatures are a result of the extreme precipitation deficit during the winter months, with the resulting aridity leading to an increased diurnal temperature variation.

## Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sports")]

Potosí is home to football teams [Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Potos%C3%AD "Real Potosí") and [Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacional_Potos%C3%AD "Nacional Potosí"), which play their matches at the 32,000-capacity multi-purpose stadium [Estadio Víctor Agustín Ugarte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_V%C3%ADctor_Agust%C3%ADn_Ugarte "Estadio Víctor Agustín Ugarte"), one of the highest stadiums in the world.

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Transportation")]

The city is served by [Aeropuerto Capitán Nicolas Rojas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Nicolas_Rojas_Airport "Captain Nicolas Rojas Airport"), with commercial airline flights by [Boliviana de Aviación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boliviana_de_Aviaci%C3%B3n "Boliviana de Aviación"), Bolivia's flag air carrier. There is also a railroad, the [Rio Mulatos-Potosí line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Mulatos-Potos%C3%AD_line "Rio Mulatos-Potosí line").

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potos%C3%AD&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Legacy")]

The city of [San Luis Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Luis_Potos%C3%AD_(city) "San Luis Potosí (city)") in Mexico was named after Potosí in Bolivia. In the United States, the name Potosi was optimistically given to lead-mining towns of [Potosi, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Wisconsin "Potosi, Wisconsin"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD#cite_note-49) and [Potosi, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Missouri "Potosi, Missouri"), and also to the silver-mining town of [Potosi, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi,_Nevada "Potosi, Nevada").
